#5032. Lido tightens Ethereum staking penalties as operators gain access to larger validators

Lido voters approved broader penalties to recover missed Ethereum staking rewards and other losses from operators’ collateral.

Lido voters backed a proposal on Nov. 23 to let the committee overseeing its two community staking modules recover more Ethereum staking losses from operators’ bonds.

In the March slashing case that prompted the vote, Lido’s contracts automatically recovered about 43% of the loss, while the operator voluntarily covered the rest.

The Snapshot result posted on Lido’s governance forum showed 53.8 million LDO in favor and 4.1 million against, enough to reach quorum. The off-chain vote backed a wider remit for the committee overseeing Lido’s two open-entry Community Staking Modules, 0x01 and 0x02.

The vote carried zero on-chain actions, so individual penalties must still be reported and settled separately.

The updated mandate extends an existing penalty mechanism used when operators divert block rewards. It would also cover staking rewards missed after slashing, along with incidents that could harm the protocol, such as withdrawal delays or risks to validator key security.

Committee members who backed the change called for documented evidence, credit for losses already recovered, and a chance for operators to respond.

Lido’s final incident report put the March 12 slashing at 0.7973122 ETH in penalties and missed rewards. When the six validators withdrew, Lido’s contracts automatically took 0.3459189 ETH from the operator’s bond to cover the withdrawal shortfall.

The operator voluntarily paid the remaining 0.4513933 ETH after the committee made contact, and Lido reported that the incident was fully resolved in April.

Lido published its final loss figures on April 22.

The amount Lido could collect at settlement would depend on the bond still available.

This graphic describes one resolved incident. Percentages are rounded.

Use Lido’s April 22 final accounting for the March 12 incident. Divide each reported amount by 0.7973122 ETH and round to the nearest whole percent for labels. Bar segment widths use the unrounded shares.

This graphic describes one resolved incident. Percentages are rounded.

In a similar case under the wider mandate, the committee could assess the missed rewards separately and lock collateral against that amount. The amount Lido could collect at settlement would depend on the bond left after the automatic deduction.

Please enable JavaScript to verify and send this form.

Under the penalty procedure, the report locks the assessed loss and any applicable fine, and the operator can compensate Lido or dispute the report. The committee can start an Easy Track motion to settle the penalty.

The locked collateral is burned when the motion is enacted, and Lido’s Easy Track rules give LDO holders at least 72 hours to object. Objections backed by at least 0.5% of total LDO supply stop the motion.

The bond backs all validators run under the same operator account in a module. Lido sizes the required collateral by the number of keys the operator runs.

In 0x01, a default operator posts 2.4 ETH for the first 32 ETH validator and 1.3 ETH for each additional key. The 0x02 module requires 32 ETH for the first key and 30 ETH for each additional key.

A 0x02 validator receives 32 ETH to start and can receive more stake after activation without increasing the required bond.

At the theoretical 2,048 ETH effective-balance ceiling, the 32 ETH first-key bond would equal about 1.56% of that balance. The 2.4 ETH first-key bond in 0x01 equals 7.5% of the validator’s 32 ETH balance.

Lido launched 0x02 on Oct. 23, and its October operator update reported nearly 800,000 ETH being validated in the established module. The first 30 keys in 0x02 had received seed deposits, or 960 ETH in all, with 54 more keys still queued at the time.

Kvorum’s record of a separate Nov. 18 motion shows the 0x02 allocation limit rose from 0.01% to 0.5% of Lido’s core pool. The higher limit lets the module take on more stake as deposits arrive.

Lido’s operator documentation says the collateral is held in stETH. If an assessed penalty exceeds the available bond, the excess becomes debt that can be recovered from future rewards or bond top-ups.

Queued keys that lose bond coverage stop receiving deposits, and unbonded validators can face exit requests. How much and how quickly the protocol can recover depends on what the operator has left in the bond and what comes in later.

#5031. XRP Exchange Inflows Hit 4.61 Billion in 30 Days

XRP has continued to see traders deposit large amounts of tokens into exchanges, including Binance, Bybit and others, as the prolonged market volatility has triggered increased fear across the broader crypto market.

Latest data from the crypto analytics platform CryptoQuant shows that about 4.61 billion XRP have flowed into crypto exchanges over the last 30 days.

According to the data, Binance has led all other crypto exchanges in the amount of XRP inflows received over the last month as its users appear to have panicked amid rising market struggles.

As such, Binance recorded about 1.221 billion XRP deposits during the period, representing the lion's share of the total inflows.

Ranking second on the list is OKX, which followed with about 866.51 million XRP, while Bybit was next with 662.57 million XRP.

The trend extended to other exchanges, even though they saw considerably lower inflows: Upbit saw about 176.96 million XRP flow into its exchange during the same period, while Bitget recorded inflows of about 140.02 million XRP.

Although the past month has seen billions of XRP transferred back to exchanges, further data shows that the 4.6 billion XRP inflow is substantially lower when compared with inflows seen in October.

In October, the total XRP that flowed into exchanges throughout the month was estimated at around 6 billion XRP, suggesting that XRP selling pressure has eased compared with the previous month.

This has drawn attention across the crypto market as the price of XRP suffered larger losses this month compared with last month, sparking questions about whether investor confidence is recovering.

#5029. Best Crypto Wallets: Top 7 Picks for Max Security and Ease of Use

Home » Cryptopedia » Best Crypto Wallets: Top 7 Picks for Max Security and Ease of Use

Compare the top hardware and software crypto wallets to find your safest, easiest self-custody setup.

Keeping your cryptocurrency on an exchange is convenient, but it comes with risks. If the exchange gets hacked, freezes withdrawals, or runs into financial trouble, accessing your funds can become difficult. Using a self-custody wallet gives you direct control over your private keys and, ultimately, your crypto.

Whether you are holding Bitcoin for the next decade, trading memecoins on Solana, or exploring decentralized finance (DeFi), choosing the right wallet matters. Some wallets are designed to keep your assets as secure as possible, while others make it easier to trade, manage tokens, and connect to Web3 apps.

To help you find the right option, we’ve put together a list of seven popular crypto wallets, covering what each one does best, its main advantages, and what to consider before choosing it.

*Prices change frequently, so always confirm on the manufacturer’s official website.

If your primary goal is long-term wealth preservation, Ledger remains the industry benchmark for cold storage.

Unlike mobile apps that stay connected to the internet, Ledger devices store your private keys inside an offline, certified Secure Element chip, the same class of chip used in passports and credit cards (check Ledger’s website for the current certification details).

Through the Ledger Live companion app, you can buy, swap, and stake thousands of coins and tokens. Your private keys never leave the device. Ledger Live runs on your connected phone or computer, but transactions are signed on the Ledger itself.

For those who live by the motto “don’t trust, verify,” Trezor is the gold standard. Contrary to the competitors that keep parts of their code proprietary, Trezor’s firmware is fully open-source, meaning independent security researchers constantly audit it for vulnerabilities.

The Trezor Safe 5 pairs this transparency with a vibrant color touchscreen, haptic feedback, and an EAL6+ Secure Element. It also offers a dedicated Bitcoin-only firmware option for maximalists who want to minimize attack surfaces.

When it comes to interacting with decentralized applications (DApps), decentralized exchanges (DEXs), and NFT marketplaces, MetaMask is the undisputed gateway to Web3.

Available as both a browser extension and a mobile app, MetasMask connects seamlessly to virtually every Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) network, including Arbitrum, Optimism, Polygon, Base, and BNB Chain.

Modern updates have expanded MetaMask beyond Ethereum via MetaMask Snaps and allow users to add support for non-EVM ecosystems like Bitcoin and Solana directly inside the same interface.

Originally built as the flagship wallet for the Solana ecosystem, Phantom has evolved into one of the fastest, cleanest multi-chain wallets on the market. Today, it seamlessly supports Solana, Ethereum, Base, Polygon, and Bitcoin in a single unified interface.

What sets Phantom apart is user experience. Transaction simulations show you exact balance changes before you hit approve, and its automated spam filter hides malicious airdrop NFTs so beginners don’t accidentally click phishing links.

If you want one smartphone app that holds virtually every cryptocurrency in existence without manual network configuration, Trust Wallet is built for you.

Supporting over 100 blockchains and millions of digital assets, it removes the technical friction of adding custom RPC networks or hunting down token contract addresses.

It also includes a built-in Web3 browser, straightforward in-app staking for major proof-of-stake coins, and an integrated Security Scanner that flags risky smart contracts.

Many newcomers confuse the main Coinbase exchange app with Coinbase Wallet, but they are completely separate products. Coinbase Wallet is a true non-custodial wallet—meaning you hold your own 12-word recovery phrase, and Coinbase cannot freeze or access your funds.

Note that the app’s branding has changed recently: Coinbase renamed it “Base App” in July 2025 and restored the Coinbase Wallet name in September 2026. It has since shifted toward multichain trading, including perpetual futures, prediction markets, and tokenized stocks, so some of its features are now aimed at more active traders.

Its biggest advantage is frictionless onboarding. You can link your exchange account to transfer funds into self-custody in seconds, claim a free human-readable username instead of copying long hexadecimal addresses, and explore Base and Ethereum DApps.

Traditional hardware wallets require cables, batteries, and carefully guarding a 24-word paper backup. Tangem reimagines cold storage as a sleek, waterproof smart card—roughly the size and thickness of a standard bank debit card.

To approve a transaction, you simply tap the card against the back of your NFC-enabled smartphone. Tangem comes in sets of two or three cards that act as physical backups for one another, allowing you to skip vulnerable paper seed phrases entirely (though a traditional seed option is still available if you prefer it).

Understanding the difference between hot and cold storage saves you from overpaying—or worse, leaving your funds exposed:

A common rule of thumb among experienced crypto investors is to use both, for example keeping around 90% of long-term holdings in a cold wallet and about 10% in a hot wallet for everyday trading and Web3 exploration. This is a guideline, not a standard – adjust it to your own situation.

With crypto, there’s no bank to call if something goes wrong. Transactions are usually irreversible, and if an exchange freezes withdrawals or goes bankrupt, your funds could be stuck for months or even years.

That’s why choosing the best crypto wallet matters. It gives you more control over your money and lets you manage your funds without relying on an exchange.

Your cryptocurrency is not stored inside the physical device—it lives on the blockchain. If your Ledger, Trezor, or Tangem card is lost, stolen, or broken, you can buy a replacement device and restore full access to your funds in minutes using your 12- or 24-word recovery phrase (or backup Tangem card).

While no system is 100% immune, cold hardware wallets cannot be hacked remotely because your private keys stay offline. Most wallet “hacks” happen when users accidentally sign a malicious smart contract on a phishing website or store their seed phrase digitally where malware can find it.

Software wallets like MetaMask, Phantom, and Trust Wallet are completely free to download and hold crypto in. Hardware wallets require an upfront purchase (typically $55 to $250). Regardless of the wallet you choose, you will still pay standard blockchain network (“gas”) fees whenever you send or swap tokens.

With a custodial wallet (like a standard exchange account), a third-party company holds your private keys and can freeze or restrict your withdrawals. With a non-custodial (self-custody) wallet, only you hold the private keys—meaning nobody can block your transactions, though you are solely responsible for backing up your recovery phrase.

No. Unlike traditional bank accounts, funds in a self-custody crypto wallet are not covered by government deposit insurance like the FDIC or SIPC. Because you act as your own bank, protecting your recovery phrase and verifying transaction details before approving them is your primary safeguard.

#5028. Crypto host who once promoted a $50 billion memecoin vision now tells traders to get out

Ansem’s wallet hack exposed security risks at Bullpen and prompted renewed debate over crypto's reputation.

Jonah, co-host of the 1000x podcast, wrote on Nov. 24 to “get out while you still can” after crypto trader Ansem said his wallet had been hacked.

Jonah predicted that staying in crypto would carry a stigma. At 03:07 UTC on Nov. 25, trading app Bullpen said the known impact of its breach was limited to 19 early beta accounts.

At 03:53 UTC, Ansem advised users to withdraw their funds until he could confidently say they were safe.

Ansem’s initial post said he suspected that someone had accessed the Bullpen profile where he had imported the private key for a Solana wallet he used on Pump.fun, and Jonah’s quote-post came in response to that claim.

Bullpen’s first public notice came later Tuesday and identified Ansem as one of the users affected.

In its initial notice, Bullpen gave a preliminary range of 18 to 19 affected accounts, all opened between April and June 2024. The company said it took the affected test service offline.

Its Wednesday update gave a figure of 19 accounts and said it had seen no further movement of the funds at that point.

Bullpen said the attacker took over the older accounts, exposing wallets users had imported into them. For users who had imported a wallet, the access Bullpen described extended beyond the trading app to funds in that wallet.

The private key Ansem said he imported could authorize transfers from the wallet he used on Pump.fun. The company said 99.8% of the funds taken came from one account, which it did not name.

Bullpen added that it was working with the FBI and other authorities, along with the services involved, to freeze and recover the funds. Ansem said he tried to freeze the money while it was still in USDC, but the attempt required a court order.

The updates describe efforts to recover the money and leave the recovered amount undisclosed.

In his follow-up, Ansem said two of his Solana wallets were compromised, identifying them as the wallet he imported from Pump.fun and a wallet already on Bullpen.

He attributed the breach to a weakness in older accounts that he said let someone bypass Bullpen’s two-factor login. Ansem also said a separate BitGo wallet requiring multiple signatures, which he said held 49% of the ANSEM token supply, was safe and unmoved.

An ANSEM sell-off unfolded on Nov. 24, driven by a large ANSEM sell-off from a publicly labeled wallet. Bitquery reported about $2.57 million in USDC at one Arbitrum address at 17:00 UTC that day.

Jonah’s comments drew a quote-post from user soby and a “This you?” reply from @CupOJoseph. In another reply, Jonah said he liked Ansem and had helped launch a token a couple of years earlier.

Jonah had published a BODEN roadmap in April 2024. The post imagined the memecoin listing on the New York Stock Exchange at a $50 billion valuation and becoming a reserve currency.

In a separate post early Wednesday, he distinguished between launching a token he considered worthless and selling it, which he said made someone a scammer.

In his own post Tuesday, 1000x co-host Avi Felman wrote that “crypto is fine,” arguing the industry grew stronger through previous downturns.

#5027. Morgan Stanley Shares $1.96 Trillion Portfolio Update: Heavy Bitcoin Focus, XRP Exposure

Morgan Stanley has disclosed its latest crypto-related holdings in a quarterly Form 13F filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. According to the filing, the bank's U.S. equity portfolio was valued at around $1.96 trillion as of Sept. 30, up from $1.89 trillion at the end of June.

Most of the crypto-related positions in the filing are Bitcoin products and Bitcoin-linked stocks, and the bank also reported a small amount of XRP exposure through three spot exchange-traded funds.

The largest crypto-related position in the filing is Strategy (MSTR). Morgan Stanley held around 10.88 million MSTR shares worth about $1.67 billion at the end of September, up from 9.33 million shares at the end of the second quarter.

The bank also increased its position in BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) from 16.48 million to 19.52 million shares, and the IBIT stake was worth about $924 million as of Sept. 30.

Besides, Morgan Stanley reported 6.72 million units of its own Morgan Stanley Bitcoin Trust (MSBT), up from 2.57 million units at the end of June. In the second-quarter filing, the MSBT position was worth about $43.3 million. MSBT started trading on NYSE Arca in April, and it was the first spot Bitcoin ETF issued by a major U.S. bank.

Among crypto stocks, Morgan Stanley also held around 10.54 million Robinhood (HOOD) shares worth about $1.19 billion and 3.72 million Coinbase (COIN) shares worth about $694 million.

Morgan Stanley reported $116,097 in XRP ETF holdings as of Sept. 30. Franklin's XRP fund accounted for $111,885 of that amount, REX-Osprey's fund for $3,098, and the Bitwise XRP ETF for the remaining $1,114.

The bank held the same three funds at the end of June. In the second quarter, Morgan Stanley reported 6,715 shares of the Franklin fund, 255 shares of the REX-Osprey fund and 67 shares of the Bitwise fund. Before that, the bank's first-quarter filing showed 1,700 shares of the Volatility Shares XRP ETF and 100 shares of the Grayscale XRP Trust ETF worth $15,488 in total.

On Wednesday, XRP was trading at around $0.908, down 2.23% over 24 hours, according to CoinMarketCap.

Morgan Stanley was one of seven banks that disclosed XRP-linked ETF holdings in third-quarter 13F filings. The positions of the seven banks totaled about $29.4 million as of Sept. 30, and Italy's Intesa Sanpaolo accounted for $27.21 million of that amount.

Goldman Sachs reported much larger XRP positions. The bank's XRP ETF holdings rose from $87 million in the second quarter to $144 million in the third quarter, and Goldman's crypto portfolio was worth around $2.64 billion in total.

#5026. Why Nvidia Needed Jensen Huang Back—And What His Return Really Changes

Why Nvidia Needed Jensen Huang Back—And What His Return Really Changes

Jensen Huang did not unveil a breakthrough chip on Monday. He simply got his old job back—and Nvidia shares surged more than 30%, while the Nasdaq jumped nearly 7% in midday trading.

The reaction revealed something more consequential than Wall Street’s fondness for a charismatic CEO: investors had spent 11 days confronting how much of the AI boom runs through one person.

Huang, who resigned November 12 amid revelations about extramarital affairs and an unproven Chinese espionage allegation involving a former customer executive, has returned as CEO, president, and director.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Nvidia with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Nvidia’s board says his reinstatement poses no national security risk, based partly on input from senior U.S. officials. Its independent investigation, however, is not over.

The company did not stop making chips. CFO Colette Kress became interim CEO, Harvey Jones took over as Nvidia’s first board chairman, and executives insisted the technology roadmap and customer commitments remained intact.

Kress presided over earnings that showed roughly $116 billion in quarterly sales and projected about $130 billion for the following quarter—staggering numbers that still failed to calm the market.

Inside Nvidia, the transition looked considerably less routine. During the first companywide meeting without Huang, staff had submitted about 700 questions, many concerning compensation and board transparency.

Kress promised pay increases and extra stock awards in December, months earlier than planned. Executives took turns assuring workers that the company could serve customers without Huang; some employees nevertheless discussed leaving if his absence became permanent.

The pushback extended outside headquarters. An online petition gathered roughly 200,000 names, though signers’ claimed employee or shareholder affiliations were not independently verified. Altimeter Capital’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker, whose firms had disclosed about $2.1 billion in Nvidia shares, urged a deliberate succession process that kept Huang’s return possible. It was an unusual message to directors searching for a replacement: don't rush to replace the founder.

This letter was sent to Nvidia's board today.

Absolutely share @altcap belief that this letter outlines minimum acceptable standards. pic.twitter.com/ST2f5TMAa1

— Gavin Baker (@GavinSBaker) November 14, 2026

In other words, Nvidia couldn’t survive the scandal—not the one about Huang cheating, but the one about Huang leaving.

Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and turned graphics processors into the hardware behind modern AI. But his power also lies in the relationships surrounding those chips: cloud giants buying entire data centers of GPUs, developers locked into Nvidia’s CUDA software, suppliers building its next systems and policymakers deciding which markets it can serve.

Reuters reports that he has overseen roughly 60 direct reports and personally shaped major deals and product decisions.

He has also become a financier and ambassador for the AI ecosystem. Nvidia has invested in companies including CoreWeave and Nebius, which buy computing hardware to rent AI capacity to others.

That web of investment, sales, and financing is precisely why his disappearance unnerved markets far beyond Nvidia. After his outsting, Chinese customers delayed or canceled orders while leadership was unsettled; the whole Nasdaq index and the wider S&P500 crashed and odds for a bubble pop spiked to more than 70% on prediction markets.

Then, on Monday, minutes after his return, CoreWeave and Nebius shares each jumped more than 20% alongside Nvidia which had its best day in history—Huang also probably had his best day ever, too.

To have a grasp of Huang’s influence, one just needs to follow the money.

Elon Musk backed the reinstatement campaign; Y Combinator chief Garry Tan and Epic Games’ Tim Sweeney were among other prominent supporters. Bill Ackman celebrated Monday with “sanity prevails.” Trump pressed the case personally, later saying his intervention was “very important” and that the administration assured directors there was no national security obstacle to Huang’s return.

That backing helps explain the whiplash: On November 17, Jones said the board would not reinstate Huang, citing conduct inconsistent with Nvidia’s standards. Six days later, the same directors voted unanimously to bring him back. They say meetings satisfied them about his candor and leadership, but have not explained exactly what changed. Supporters see recognition of an indispensable founder; critics see a board yielding to powerful outsiders.

Bullish analysts argue that restoring Huang reduces execution and talent-retention risk. Dan Ives has framed Nvidia as a $300 stock with Huang versus $225 without him, while Melius Research upgraded the shares to “buy” with a $220 target.

Yet Monday’s roughly 30%-plus rebound followed a Friday close of $125.53; even near $165, Nvidia remains well below its October peak. Buying the comeback means paying much more for the same projected chip sales.

The other side is harder to price. Michael Burry criticized the reversal, and legal scrutiny of Huang, Nvidia’s export controls and its board continues. The company is establishing a board committee for national security and export-control oversight and recruiting a chief compliance officer.

None of that resolves the fundamental AI question: whether customers can earn enough on massive infrastructure spending to sustain Nvidia’s growth.

Huang’s return repairs a missing link between Nvidia, its customers, Wall Street, and Washington. The 11-day crisis showed how much confidence that link carries—and how vulnerable the AI trade becomes when it breaks.

What he has not yet won back is an unquestioned mandate to lead.

#5025. French Senate Rejects Disclosure Rule for Crypto

French senators on Nov. 24 rejected a proposal that would have required taxpayers to disclose self-hosted cryptocurrency holdings exceeding €100,000.

They would have had to report those assets as of Dec. 31.

This would have been the case even if they had held the same coins since January without making any sales.

Two matching amendments to the French 2027 budget were rejected by the Senate during the first reading of the draft.

Senators Pascal Savoldelli and Anne-Sophie Romagny reintroduced the proposal after it briefly passed in the National Assembly earlier in the month.

French taxpayers must disclose their crypto assets held on foreign crypto platforms.

These amendments would have expanded disclosure requirements to wallets that owners directly control. This pertains to a wallet that is not managed by an exchange or another custodian.

The French National Assembly approved the €100,000 disclosure threshold in a 150-44 vote on Nov. 3. There were also eight abstentions.

The next day, the National Assembly voted down the entire revenue portion of the budget.

This vote brought down the wallet disclosure provision along with the rest of the budget.

However, the subsequent effort to revive the provision in the Senate was defeated.

It should be noted that the 2027 budget is still being considered at the time of writing.

The Senate also rejected two other crypto-related measures debated as part of the budget.

One was a provision to tax gains realized when holders exchange cryptocurrencies for certain stablecoins.

The second was a proposal to expand France's exit tax to include unrealized gains on cryptocurrencies held by taxpayers who move their tax residence outside the country.

#5024. How Sculpt Became the Fitness Space’s Buzziest—and Vaguest—Workout

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

It’s on every class schedule and all over your feed. So what does “sculpt” actually mean, and what can it do for you?

By definition, the term sculpt means making something by carving stone or molding clay. It’s an art form, a manipulation of material to achieve a desired end result that’s aesthetically appealing.

Over the years, however, the term has also become ubiquitous in fitness culture. We talk about sculpting one's back or legs, implying some kind of crafting of muscles, as if treating the human form like a sculpture. In fact, check the group class schedule of any gym these days, and you’ll likely spot the term “sculpt” appear somewhere on the lineup—directing toward some variation of a Pilates mat or strength training class, often involving lower weights and higher reps.

Now, the term is prolific in fitness classes and social media alike, that the meaning is a bit murky—which begs the question, what does “sculpt” really mean in the context of exercise? Is it a legitimate term or nothing more than strategic marketing language?

The exercise term actually dates back decades, with the first mentions appearing in fitness publications in the late 1970s. “It comes out of bodybuilding culture, which became more prominent in that period […] and you started to see the term ‘body sculpture,’” says Natalia Mehlman Petrezela, PhD, a historian and author of Fit Nation: The Gains and Pains of America’s Exercise Obsession. And while there’s no clear record of who coined the term in a fitness context, there is speculation that it may have been inspired by German strongman Eugen Sandow (often called the "father of modern bodybuilding"), who referenced Greco-Roman sculptures as examples of the “ideal” physique in the late 19th century.

In the 1980s, the idea of sculpting your muscles started to become much more mainstream, with the rise of aerobics, toning workouts, and fitness videos, says physical therapist and trainer Shannon Ritchey, PT, DPT, founder of Evlo Fitness. As instructors began using the term to describe and market workouts designed to shape and define specific muscles, “sculpting” became part of the everyday fitness vocabulary.

The term also taps into something more personal: this idea that we have the power to change the shape of our own physiques. “I think that it really gained momentum because one, it kind of speaks to the artistry of the body or the artistry of fitness. Also, there's so much individual agency in this,” says Petrezela. “It isn't about you just having the right genetics. Instead, you as an artist have the power to sculpt your own body.”

In the 1990s, however, the revered muscular look brought about by ’80s fitness culture made way for a celebration of thinner, more waifish bodies. “There was—and this is still the case—a lot of fear around getting too bulky,” says Petrezela. The term sculpting, however, molded into a promise of strength training without gaining too much muscle, which felt more palatable to women who feared such a physique.

“What's interesting is that we've changed the language over the years, but we're still selling women a very similar idea: that certain exercises will create a long, lean, toned appearance, while others will make them bulky,” says Ritchey.

If you worked out in the 2010s, you probably remember “sculpt” becoming a fixture of the boutique fitness boom. Still, while studio culture has waxed and waned over the last 20 years, the term has only gained traction, popping up across social media and on class schedules everywhere (think Pilates sculpt, yoga sculpt, and seemingly endless variations), notes Laura Girard, CPT, a NASM personal trainer and co-host of the Fit Literate podcast.

Girard speculates that the popularity of sculpt classes may be buoyed by the widespread craving for more community in a post-pandemic world. After all, group fitness can be a fantastic third space. But there's another reason “sculpt” makes for such an appealing class name: It signals a particular kind of workout experience. Girard has observed “sculpt” used “almost like a dog whistle that [suggests] this class is going to be friendly for women and not scary, but still intense,” she says.

There's an aesthetic appeal, too. Petrezela believes the term’s resurgence of sorts has to do with how weightlifting and building muscle are very much having a moment, yet longstanding fears around getting “bulky” haven’t entirely disappeared. “It doesn't hurt that we are in a very, very image-driven moment in fitness culture,” she says. “We're not just looking at the images in magazines that come out once a month, but our [social media] feeds are nonstop bodies all day—many of which are shared by influencers who have their own plans for how you can sculpt a body that looks just like theirs, or so they say.”

If you were to ask 10 different people on the street what a “sculpt class” is, you may get 10 different answers. To some, sculpt is synonymous with a mat Pilates routine, to others it might be a strength-training session, and to others it might be a yoga practice involving light dumbbells. So, can all of these workouts really fall under the same umbrella? And when a class promises to “sculpt,” is that an actual measurable result your muscles can deliver—or a feeling the name is designed to sell?

According to the experts, it’s largely the latter. “In a world where two things are popular—strength training and being very thin—’sculpting’ seems to be an appealing middle ground from a marketing perspective,” says Ritchey. “It promises ‘long, lean muscle tone’ without the perceived risk of building too much muscle.”

She adds that “sculpt” is often used interchangeably with “toning,” which she describes as a “made-up term” that typically refers to changing your body composition (a.k.a., reducing fat and building muscle).

Because there's no single definition, what you actually do in a sculpt class can vary considerably. Still, Girard notes many sculpt classes share certain characteristics: lighter weights, choreography-inspired movements, and a lot of mat work. She also notes that while exercises are often fatiguing (think: that familiar muscle-burning sensation), they’re not necessarily pushing you to muscle failure via progressive overload (which is necessary for hypertrophy, or muscle-building).

Ritchey, who taught a sculpt class years ago, recalls using dumbbells and bodyweight for high reps. “We would do an entire three- to four-minute song of squats and lunges. That’s likely over 100 squats in a row, which burns and feels hard,” she says. Of course, it’s certainly possible to promote muscle-building with a low-weight, high-rep range, granted the programming is intentional. “But we know that if you could physically do more than about 30 reps in a row, the load is too light to build muscle.”

It’s important to note that a workout doesn't have to maximize muscle growth to be worthwhile. Certain sculpt classes can offer other benefits, from muscular endurance to simply providing motivation and enjoyment of exercising, often in a group setting. But if your primary goal is to significantly increase muscle size or change your body composition, not every sculpt class will provide the progressive resistance training needed to make that happen.

That’s where experts say the “sculpt” terminology can get confusing or misleading for some people. Girard fears that the language surrounding sculpt workouts reinforces misconceptions about women's bodies and what exercise can realistically change. “Sculpt as a verb is not a thing we can do to our bodies,” she notes. “We can gain or lose muscle. We can gain or lose fat, but that's more the role of nutrition. But we can't control how those muscles look.”

In other words, there's no special exercise technique that creates “long, lean” muscles instead of so-called “bulky” ones. Your genetics influence your muscle shape, while your training can affect how much muscle you build. And the workout's name doesn't change those underlying principles.

What’s more, at a time when there’s seemingly no consensus on how to talk about bodies or fitness in an empowering, nonoffensive way, Girard sees the term “sculpt” as potential coded language. While we may have mostly done away with, say, “bikini body shred” language in 2026, she fears that this nebulous term may be subliminally hinting at the same idea.

And while there's absolutely “nothing wrong with having aesthetic goals,” Ritchey stresses, “women deserve accurate information about how to achieve them.” If body recomp is their goal, they would have more success lifting close to failure and focusing on diet.”

Ultimately, your muscles don’t know whether you’re in a sculpt class or a traditional strength workout. Instead, they respond to the resistance, effort, and progression involved.

“It’s funny because while all these trends come and go—and we will see sculpt come and go, too—the science never changes,” Ritchey says. “People just aren’t patient enough with the basics, so they jump on the latest trend thinking it will finally be the golden ticket to seeing results.”

Because “sculpt” has no one definition, the quality, intensity, and overall experience of classes bearing the name can vary widely, too.

Beyond the workout itself, Girard points out that some sculpt classes can come with an unspoken expectation about who belongs in the room. As she’s observed: “These classes tend to be a self-selecting in-group. You may only see one type of body, or one specific outfit [...] That doesn’t mean it’s wrong or bad to be in a different outfit or in a different body, but it sure can feel that way.”

Of course, there are also plenty of classes with “sculpt” in the name that are fantastic, inclusive workouts. This all boils down to the instructor, methods, and specific exercises they choose to incorporate—along with the type of community they cultivate. And, in many cases—particularly with larger studios or gyms—instructors have no say in what their class is actually called. “A lot of times, they're just doing what's trending to get people in the door,” says Girard.

So if you’ve been curious to try a new sculpt class at a local studio—by all means, go for it. Just be sure to go into it with eyes wide open, and give yourself permission to stop or pause or walk away if it doesn’t feel like a productive or positive environment for you. Pay attention to how the workout feels, how the instructor coaches, and whether the environment makes you feel welcome. One potential red flag? Aggressive “bikini body” messaging or marketing that frames building muscle as something to avoid. As Girard emphasizes, “It is definitely, definitely is not.”

As the experts agree: Finding a form of movement you enjoy is the most important ingredient for establishing a healthy, consistent fitness routine. “My advice would be to ask yourself why you're doing these classes. Is it because you genuinely enjoy them? Or is it because you believe the burning sensation means you're toning and sculpting your muscles? Because those are two very different things,” says Ritchey.

Have a sculpt workout you absolutely love? That’s wonderful, too. Finding movement you genuinely enjoy is one of the best ways to build a fitness routine you'll actually stick with. The important thing is understanding what you're getting out of it—and whether that aligns with what you're hoping to achieve.

“I want women to feel empowered to choose exercise based on what they enjoy and what actually works,” says Ritchey.

For someone primarily focused on building muscle, Ritchey recommends treating sculpt classes as opportunities for cardio or simply enjoyable movement, rather than as a replacement for progressive strength training.

They can even be great options for off days from lifting. “I don’t want to discourage anyone from moving,” she says. “But at the same time, we deserve to understand what is marketing and what our bodies actually respond to. We are all busy and tired and stressed [and] I want women to know how to best use their efforts to match their goals.”

Appreciate the workout for what it is, understand what it isn't, and choose what works for you. That, in fact, is the true artistry of exercise.

Natalia Mehlman Petrezela, PhD, is a professor of history at the New School and author of Fit Nation: The Gains and Pains of America’s Exercise Obsession. Shannon Ritchey, PT, DPT, is a physical therapist, fitness instructor, and founder of Evlo Fitness. Laura Girard, CPT, is a NASM-certified personal trainer, founder of The Energy Academy, and co-host of the Fit Literate podcast.

Kristine Thomason is a writer and editor with over a decade of experience creating content for print and digital publications. Previously, she was the health and fitness director at mindbodygreen, and the fitness and wellness editor at Women’s Health. Kristine's work has appeared in Men's Health, Travel + Leisure, Health, and Refinery29, among others. She holds a journalism degree from New York University, and is certified in personal training by the National Academy of Sports Medicine (NASM).

#5023. Bitcoin Falls as PCE Inflation Comes in Hotter Than Expected

Home » Bitcoin (BTC) » Bitcoin Falls as PCE Inflation Comes in Hotter Than Expected

Heavy ETF outflows, surging put bets, and fragile support leave traders watching whether a deeper slide is just beginning.

Bitcoin (BTC) fell below $60,000 on Wednesday, trading at around $58,220 as concerns about further losses grew ahead of Thanksgiving. The BTC price dropped 2.8% in 24 hours following the release of October inflation data, which showed that price pressures remained elevated according to the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation measure.

The U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) reported that the October Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index rose 0.3% in October, matching September’s increase.

Core PCE inflation, which excludes food and energy, climbed 0.3% on the month and 3.3% from a year earlier. Headline PCE inflation increased 3.8% from a year earlier.

The report also showed that US personal income rose 0.7% in October, while consumer spending increased 0.3%. However, real consumer spending was virtually unchanged, suggesting that higher prices continued to weigh on purchasing power.

Bitcoin price fell to about $55,300 over the weekend before recovering to around $64,400 on Tuesday on renewed stock market optimism after Nvidia reinstated its CEO, Jensen Huang.

However, the major crypto “acted as the canary in the coal mine”, according to Glassnode: BTC fully gave back the NVIDIA-driven rally within hours while stocks lagged, then came under pressure. Price broke the $62,000–66,000 support zone, retested summer lows, and is struggling to hold around the $60,000 level.

Bitcoin lost nearly 26% of its value over the past 30 days, and the realized losses are the heaviest since the FTX crash in November 2022.

In addition to that, approximately 90% of the tracked leveraged long positions between the previous week’s market price and Bitcoin’s realized price ($53,200) have been liquidated.

Glassnode suggests that much of the selling pressure is coming from the US. Over the past 20 trading days, US spot Bitcoin ETFs have seen around $4.3 billion in net outflows, marking one of their biggest periods of withdrawals since launch.

Spot market activity tells a similar story: over the past 30 days, US investors on Coinbase have been net sellers, while buying and selling on Binance have remained relatively balanced.

Glassnode’s latest data shows growing bearishness among Bitcoin options traders, with limited support against sharp price movements around current levels. Between $58K and $64K, options dealers are positioned in a way that could amplify volatility, potentially accelerating a sell-off if prices fall further.

Meanwhile, bearish bets are rising. Traders bought 1.7 put options for every call last week, the highest ratio since June 2022. Similar levels of pessimism appeared near Bitcoin’s 2022 market low, although prices continued falling for several more months.

Glassnode warns that Bitcoin’s current decline may not be over. Bitcoin price remains weaker than traditional equities, US buying demand is lacking, and the market is struggling to hold its summer lows.

Glassnode identifies $60,000 as a key level to watch. A decisive break below it, followed by a close under $58,500, could open the door to a decline towards $53,200.

A recovery above $60,000, supported by renewed spot Bitcoin ETF inflows, would offer stronger evidence that the market is stabilising.

Shiba Inu (SHIB) kept leaving crypto exchanges this week as the price of the meme cryptocurrency fell to levels last seen in the spring of 2021, and on Wednesday, the outflow picked up sharply.

According to CoinGlass data, 520.83 billion SHIB left exchanges over the past 24 hours. That amount made up most of the 757.51 billion SHIB that exchanges lost over the past seven days, and over the past 30 days, the outflow reached 2.88 trillion SHIB.

On Wednesday evening, SHIB was trading at $0.00000344, according to CoinGlass. So far this week, the token was down 4.78%, and its market capitalization went down to $2.02 billion, according to TradingView.

According to the weekly chart on TradingView, SHIB last traded at these levels in the spring of 2021, months before the token reached its all-time high of $0.00008845 on Oct. 28, 2021.

From early 2026 until mid-November, the price of SHIB held above $0.000004, and the yearly low stood at $0.00000411 at the July 17 close. In November, SHIB fell to $0.00000373, and in late November, the token dropped as low as $0.00000337. On Jan. 1, the token closed the day at $0.00000692, and since the start of the year, SHIB has lost 50.3% of its value, according to CoinGlass. As of Nov. 22, SHIB had lost 22.7% in November so far, according to CryptoRank.

The latest drop in SHIB came after Bitcoin fell back below $60,000 this week. On Saturday, Nov. 21, Bitcoin dropped as low as $55,150, its lowest price since September 2024. Over the past 24 hours, $57,590 worth of SHIB futures positions were liquidated, and $54,750 of that amount came from long positions on OKX, according to CoinGlass.

The Wednesday outflow was not the first large one this month. On Nov. 17, about 312 billion SHIB were withdrawn from exchanges, according to CryptoQuant. On the same day, the number of SHIB holders on Ethereum passed 1.7 million, according to Etherscan.

CoinGlass data also shows that since late 2024, the total SHIB balance on exchanges has gone down by 19.18 trillion tokens, or 20.54%, to 74.19 trillion, and over the same period, the price of SHIB fell by 88.39%. The remaining 74.19 trillion SHIB on exchanges make up 12.59% of the circulating supply and are worth about $254.75 million.

Most of the 24-hour outflow came from exchanges that CoinGlass groups as "Others," as their combined SHIB balance fell by 88.5% to 70.93 billion tokens. Over the same period, the SHIB balances of Binance and OKX barely changed, and Coinbase, Bitfinex and Bitstamp added SHIB.

As a result, in the week when the price of SHIB fell to levels last seen in 2021, exchanges lost more SHIB in a single day than over the previous six days combined, according to CoinGlass data.

#5021. North Korea Moves $247 Million of Binance Hack Loot Through Bitcoin Mixers

North Korea Moves $247 Million of Binance Hack Loot Through Bitcoin Mixers

North Korea’s hackers have now funneled at least $247 million from the record $6.4 billion Binance theft through Bitcoin “coinjoins,” a mixing technique designed to sever the trail between stolen funds and their origin, blockchain analytics firm Elliptic said.

The figure, roughly a month after the Oct. 29 hack, reflects just the funds pushed into coinjoins, which pool many users’ Bitcoin into a single transaction so the coins can’t be traced.

Notably, almost all of it was coordinated by a single known individual: the operator of Kruw, the most widely used coinjoin coordinator for Wasabi Wallet users. That operator “refuses to block funds such as these,” Elliptic co-founder Tom Robinson told Decrypt in an email, which is why the firm expects the laundering to continue.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

The mixing accelerated sharply in mid-November. On Nov. 17, the attacker emptied five of the nine largest Ethereum addresses tied to the theft, shifting about 488,000 ETH ($860 million) into fresh batches.

Those are being steadily swapped into Bitcoin through the Thorchain bridge and then sent into coinjoins, often within hours, the same playbook North Korea used after the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in early 2025.

The operation has spanned more than 27,000 wallets across at least 16 blockchains, roughly 55 services and some 90,000 transactions. Elliptic stressed it is clearly automated but found no evidence AI agents are directing it, pointing instead to conventional software, with fixed timing, set amounts and pauses that resemble human working patterns in Pyongyang.

Elliptic earlier found the hackers even minted their own worthless meme coins to shuffle funds through liquidity pools, one of several obfuscation tactics stacked together alongside cross-chain bridges, asset swaps and lending-vault hops.

The FBI has attributed the theft to the North Korean group TraderTraitor, and Binance has said it will cover all customer losses.

Still, little has actually been cashed out. About $2.85 billion has been frozen, and roughly $2.35 billion remains parked in theft-linked addresses, including the 18,270 BTC taken directly from Binance, which hasn’t moved since the night of the hack.

Elliptic expects the funds to be converted to Bitcoin, mixed and eventually cashed out through over-the-counter brokers over a period of months, the point at which they can still be intercepted.

With the Kruw operator declining to block the flows, though, the mixing shows little sign of slowing.

#5020. Jennifer Lawrence’s Hair Care Brand Launch Faced Public Scrutiny—But How Do the Products Actually Perform?

I tested Mes° Beauty for two weeks to find out.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

When Jennifer Lawrence joined Instagram in September, fans rejoiced at the idea of seeing more content from the actress known for her sarcastic humor and likable authenticity. What we didn’t see coming was the launch of her new hair care brand Mes° Beauty (pronounced “mess”) and the public backlash that followed.

In an already oversaturated beauty market, celebrity brands are a dime a dozen, and the announcement of Mes° Beauty didn’t exactly land well with the public. “She saw the numbers Rihanna, Selena Gomez, and Hailey Bieber were pulling in, and suddenly decided to join Instagram, too. Not necessarily to connect with her audience, but perhaps to tap into the same commercial machine and sell us even more stuff,” wrote one Instagram commenter.

JLaw teamed up with Jasmina Aganovic, founder of biotech beauty company Arcaea Labs, to formulate the brand’s hair care. As they say, the proof is in the pudding, so when I was sent all three products in a PR mailer, I knew I wanted to put them to the test.

Read my full, honest review of Mes° Beauty’s hair mask, serum, and volume mist below.

An intensive repair mask designed to be applied to dry hair anytime before washing. The milky-colored mask has a silky yet sticky, gelatin-like consistency that clings to your hair as you apply it. According to the brand, the mask prevents breakage and wash-day protein loss and protects the hair’s lipid barrier.

The Multitask Repair Mask differs from other hair masks because you apply it before shampooing and can leave it on for five minutes or overnight. With such a wide treatment time, it might take some trial and error to find the “sweet spot” for your hair type. During my testing, I applied a generous coat of the mask 5 to 10 minutes before shampooing. The second time, I tried applying a thinner coat of the mask, then pinned my hair up with a claw clip for about two hours before rinsing it out. The longer you wear it, the better the results. I would recommend applying a light coat before going about your day; that way, the scent isn’t overpowering and it won’t drip on your clothes.

After just two uses, my hair looked shinier and felt more hydrated after styling. As someone who rarely plans my hair care routine ahead of time, I appreciate that I can apply the mask just five minutes before I hop in the shower and still get noticeable results.

Although Mes° says the mask doubles as a styler for a glossy wet-hair look, I wouldn’t use it in that way. I think the product's consistency is too sticky and would be uncomfortable and messy (literally) to wear all day.

Some reviewers have mentioned a slightly off-putting smell. While the scent doesn’t bother me (it smells like a light, musky fragrance), it may not be for everyone. If I’m paying $52 for a hair mask, it would be nice to have a luxurious fragrance to add to the experience. If a brand is going to do musk, really lean into it with notes of sandalwood, amber, or patchouli.

The packaging also makes the product difficult to use. In the mailer I received, the mask comes in a GoGo Squeez-like pouch that you’re supposed to empty into the plastic tub. However, dipping my fingers into the tub felt clumsy, and next time I would just dispense directly from the pouch.

A bi-phase serum that smooths frizz, restores shine, and provides heat protection up to 450 degrees Fahrenheit. The “bi-phase” claim comes from combining a lightweight oil and a serum in the formula. After touching it, applying it, and letting it sit in my hair for a few days, I think calling it a serum is misleading. The consistency and the way it applies are much more like a hair oil.

On day two hair, I warmed two drops of the Off-Duty Restyling Serum between my palms, and worked it through my strands. I have very thick, straight, shoulder-length hair, so when I applied the serum up through my mid-lengths, it was way too oily. I don’t know if I would use it to restyle my hair unless I was planning to use a hot tool.

I also tested the serum as a finishing product, applying it to my ends after blow-drying. I found this to be the most effective way to use the product on my hair type.

Overall, the Off-Duty Restyling Serum doesn’t make much sense to me. What’s the point of having heat protection if it’s made for “reshaping yesterday’s style?” Are we going back in with more heat? To me, that sounds like an extra step in my morning routine that I do not have the time or patience for.

On days when I wash and blow-dry my hair, I like using a tiny amount of the serum just on my ends, and I've found it dries down nicely and leaves my hair soft and touchable. That said, I own other lightweight hair oils that work just as well for a fraction of the price—like FromLabs’ Protein Capsule Hair Repair Oil. If you have fine, wavy, or curly hair, the Off-Duty Serum may work better for you.

A lightweight spray that reduces scalp oiliness for lasting lift. Instead of creating gritty texture or absorbing excess oil like a dry shampoo, the Good Roots mist helps balance the scalp microbiome to produce less oil at the roots, extending the time until your next wash.

Over the past two weeks, I tested the Good Roots mist in three ways: applying it to damp hair before blow-drying, applying it to damp hair before air-drying, and applying it to dry day-two and day-three hair.

After about five uses of trial and error, I found it worked best when I applied it to my clean, damp roots and blow-dried. The heat felt like it helped dry down and “activate” the mist, whereas letting my hair air-dry didn’t produce much volume.

Pro-Tip: Be sure to hold the bottle about a foot away for even misting. The applicator pump doesn’t produce a fine spritz, and it took me a few uses to get that right.

After two weeks of testing, the Good Roots Volume Mist is my favorite of the trio. Two key ingredients, the proprietary Arc-5 Technology and the Mediterranean microalgae, help support a balanced scalp, keeping your hair fresher longer. With consistent use, the Good Roots mist extended my time between hair washes—I typically wash every other day, but I was able to go a third day. Plus, the Juniperus virginiana oil in the formula has a fresh, woody scent that reminds me of a fancy sea salt spray.

I also like that the mist doesn’t make my hair feel super gritty or textured the way a dry shampoo might. That said, I have other dry shampoo products that do a lot more heavy lifting than this volume mist. If I’m looking to achieve noticeable volume and lift in my thick hair, the Good Roots mist doesn’t cut it.

My general critique of Mes° Beauty is that the products are not very intuitive. They seem straightforward, but the brand doesn’t give great direction on how to get the most out of them. After the first one or two uses, you may feel they barely do anything at all. But if you learn how to use them properly when styling your hair, they can perform fairly well.

Mes° is supposed to be about “Less time fixing your hair. More time living,” but in reality, achieving that effortlessly chic, tousled look requires a fair bit of effort. In my opinion, this lineup is much more suited to someone who blows out or flat irons or curls their hair once or twice a week and wants to extend their style. For my hair type, these products don’t fit into my routine in a way that makes sense, but if you have fine and/or wavy hair, they might work better for you.

Curious about my other hair standbys? They’re currently $30 and under—and make for excellent beauty gift ideas for your loved ones for the upcoming holiday season.

#5019. Franklin Templeton's Crypto ETF to Add Hyperliquid: Will HYPE Price Recover?

The Franklin Crypto Index ETF is preparing to add Hyperliquid to its portfolio, according to a prospectus supplement filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on Wednesday.

The fund currently holds Bitcoin, Ethereum, XRP, Dogecoin, Solana, Cardano and Stellar.

The HYPE token will be held in spot, with its allocation determined by its weighting in the underlying CF Benchmarks index. The fund is expected to maintain a portfolio structure broadly aligned with the index.

The move comes as major trader Abraxas Capital reportedly exited its Hyperliquid position on Wednesday. The firm is said to have generated approximately $530 million in profits from the trade.

In September, Hashdex added HYPE to its Nasdaq CME Crypto Index ETF, with a 3.36% weighting.

Currently, there are three Hyperliquid ETFs: THYP and HYPG by 21Shares, and Bitwise's BHYP. Their combined assets, however, remain relatively low, currently under $259 million.

Hyperliquid is trading near $59.8, down 1.3% over the past 24 hours and 10.2% over the previous week.

The $55-$56 range is an immediate support area. A move above $60 could signal declining selling pressure, while a decline below the range could lead to more liquidations and further correction.

HYPE has slipped below its major moving averages, including the 200-day moving average near $68, reinforcing the bearish outlook.

Meanwhile, the RSI hovers around 35, indicating weakening momentum and approaching oversold conditions.

The market is also preparing for an important token unlock scheduled for Dec. 6. Reports estimate that the release could be worth $578 million at current prices.

#5018. SBI brings Japanese stocks to Solana but investors face a five-day wait to cash out

SBI’s Solana expansion brings Japanese equities to more investors through USDC, with redemptions taking five dealing days.

SBI Solana Global began full-scale operations on Nov. 25, with plans to bring Japanese financial assets to more markets.

Eligible professional investors can use USDC to buy exposure to a Japanese dividend stock fund through Hong Kong’s HashKey Earn. To exit, they submit a redemption request, and HashKey expects settlement on T+5 under the issuer’s dealing calendar and settlement arrangements.

SBI Holdings, Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group and the Solana Foundation said they completed agreements for a new joint-venture structure and that the former SBI R3 Japan began operating under its new name.

The partners plan to use Solana to distribute Japanese assets and develop services in stablecoin payments, financial and real-world asset tokenization, and on-chain asset management.

The partners intend to start with practical uses in Japan before expanding across Asia and linking up with global markets.

DigiFT and SBI Global Asset Management announced the token JX on July 15. DigiFT issued the token on Solana as a depositary receipt linked to the SBI Japan High Dividend Equity Fund’s growth type, managed by SBI Asset Management.

The fund invests mainly in listed Japanese companies and seeks returns from dividends and rising share prices. DigiFT says the growth structure makes no distributions at either the fund or token level.

Qualified investors first gained access through Singapore-based DigiFT on July 14, according to SBI Global Asset Management. On Nov. 5, SBI Global Asset Management announced a second distribution channel through HashKey Earn, a service of the licensed Hong Kong platform HashKey Exchange.

That gave eligible investors a second place to buy JX while SBI Asset Management continued to run the underlying portfolio.

Clients must qualify as professional investors under HashKey and issuer rules and complete applicable onboarding and suitability checks.

The public dealing terms list a minimum subscription of 5,000 USDC and a minimum redemption of 750,000 JX tokens, and the platform lists a 0.1% redemption fee.

The daily cutoff is 9 a.m. Hong Kong time. HashKey expects settlement in five dealing days for subscriptions and redemptions after the applicable dealing date.

The final price and timing depend on the product’s valuation and settlement arrangements. A non-dealing day in Japan, Singapore, or the US can affect processing or settlement.

#5017. NYSE’s Avalanche Pick Hints At XRP’s Role

Home » Trendsetter News » NYSE’s Avalanche Pick Hints At XRP’s Role

NYSE’s reported choice of Avalanche for a tokenized-stock platform does not necessarily rule out XRP.

The New York Stock Exchange’s reported choice of Avalanche for a tokenized-stock platform does not necessarily shut out XRP, wealth commentator Kamilah Stevenson argues in her latest video.

Her distinction: settling share ownership and moving money across currencies are separate jobs, and winning one does not automatically secure the other.

According to Dr. Stevenson, Ava Labs announced that Avalanche would provide the core ledger for the clearing firm behind the proposed platform.

She cites Wall Street Journal reporting that Avalanche would be its sole settlement blockchain, with regulatory approval still required.

The proposed venue would support around-the-clock trading and near-instant settlement. Stevenson says NYSE tested Avalanche for roughly a year, prioritizing transaction speed, predictable costs and control over who can participate.

That permissioning capability matters for a regulated exchange. Avalanche (AVAX) can support customized networks with participation restrictions, rather than requiring the exchange to conduct settlement on an unrestricted public network.

AVAX rose as much as roughly 10% on the news, according to the video. Stevenson, who discloses holding the token, calls the selection a win for Avalanche, but cautions against treating infrastructure adoption as proof of investment returns.

“A network being used by a big name and its token being needed” are different things, she says. The announcement, in her account, provided neither revenue figures nor a commitment that NYSE would buy or hold AVAX.

Dr. Stevenson’s XRP thesis centers on overseas investors funding dollar-denominated stock purchases outside conventional banking hours.

A trader holding yen or another currency would need access to dollars or dollar-linked funding before buying U.S. shares.

She argues that this creates an opportunity for cross-border payment infrastructure, including XRP. But it remains a proposed use case, not a disclosed partnership: “I’m not telling you that NYSE is going to pick XRP for that.”

The YouTube video episode does not establish that XRP would be necessary for such funding. Nor does expanded trading access, by itself, demonstrate future demand for the token.

Dr. Kamilah Stevenson also says the platform would support tokenized stocks issued across multiple blockchains, distinguishing asset issuance from the ledger used for settlement.

Those details matter more than a simple Avalanche-versus-XRP contest: the unresolved questions are which services institutions actually adopt, what generates revenue, and whether that activity requires either token.

#5016. Bitcoin Sentiment Can Turn Quickly, British Strategy CEO Says

Andrew Webley, CEO of The Smarter Web Company, said that Bitcoin's drop has been sharper than he had anticipated, but he does not think the digital asset's price will decline much further.

The British CEO, whose company recently added 55 BTC to its treasury, said investors' opinions on Bitcoin can shift considerably without any changes to Bitcoin itself.

"Sentiment towards Bitcoin can change very quickly. Without Bitcoin changing at all," Webley said on X.

Webley advised investors to consider Bitcoin's movements relative to other assets. Bitcoin's price decline shows investors how much the cryptocurrency has lost in absolute terms.

However, Bitcoin's performance relative to the broader market may indicate BTC is being sold specifically or whether investors are taking profits across multiple markets. Webley did not specify which assets he was comparing Bitcoin against.

"Do I expect Bitcoin to go significantly lower from here? No. But as the past few weeks have shown, predicting short-term price movements is a very challenging task," Webley said.

Some of the most challenging periods for investors, he said, were followed by some of his most profitable periods.

His most definitive prediction concerned Bitcoin's longer-term outlook: "Bitcoin has an incredible future."

In fact, Webley's company has been buying more Bitcoin as its price has been dropping.

On Nov. 17, Smarter Web said it spent around £2.75 million on 55 BTC, bringing its total holdings to 2,905 BTC.

The average purchase price was £49,991 per Bitcoin, roughly 38% below the treasury's overall average purchase price of £81,234 following the transaction.

Smarter Web borrowed around £2.6 million under its Coinbase credit facility to finance most of the purchase. The company used its existing Bitcoin holdings as collateral.

Following the transaction, Smarter Web had around £19 million outstanding under the dollar-denominated credit facility.

#5015. Why One Math Proof Has AI Experts Warning Humans Might Soon Lose Control

Why One Math Proof Has AI Experts Warning Humans Might Soon Lose Control

Meta Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang warned Sunday that artificial superintelligence is approaching—and that humanity may be unable to control systems far smarter than itself.

In an essay on X titled “Superintelligence is Arriving,” Wang said the next year could determine how people live alongside machines capable of improving themselves. His catalyst was an extraordinary mathematics result involving Anthropic’s Claude.

“Superintelligence is arriving. How humanity acts over the next year will have great consequence on what future world we live in,” Wang wrote.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Anthropic with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Wang called the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis a greater intellectual achievement than building the atomic bomb, which he described as a “homework problem” by comparison. The breakthrough, he wrote, came with help from an “alien mind that we don’t understand.”

The warning carries extra weight because Wang runs Meta Superintelligence Labs. Mark Zuckerberg brought him aboard in 2025 after Meta invested $14.3 billion for a 49% stake in Wang’s startup, Scale AI.

On Friday, Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge said he and Claude had proved the Riemann Hypothesis, a conjecture about prime numbers that had resisted mathematicians since 1859. The claim arrived a day after Anthropic’s massive IPO.

Alpöge released roughly 17 million lines of code in Lean, a system that checks mathematical proofs. On Saturday, the Lean and Mathlib communities certified that the code proves the correct statement; researchers are still working to explain its mathematics in conventional form.

For Wang, the result suggests raw reasoning power is no longer AI’s central limitation. He argued that the remaining hurdles involve specialist knowledge, experimentation, and the tools needed to apply intelligence in other fields.

That includes AI research itself. If machines can redesign more capable successors, Wang fears a cycle of recursive self-improvement could move faster than human monitoring or intervention.

“It is hard to imagine a world where humanity can maintain control over fully unconstrained recursive self-improvement,” he wrote. He also questioned human control over hypothetical systems “1000x smarter” than people.

Wang criticized the industry’s “lazy thinking” that superintelligence is inevitable and the only question is making it safe. “We should not be okay with a ‘handover’ of society to AI,” he wrote, advocating technology that strengthens human decision-making.

In a Monday follow-up, he said Meta had delayed its Muse launch for months over safety concerns and backed industry safeguards. Zuckerberg, he added, wants most computing power devoted to serving customers rather than unrestricted self-improvement.

Meta nevertheless has its own ambitions. Its Muse Wonder models, released in October, compete with systems from OpenAI and Anthropic, making Wang both a critic of the race’s direction and a leading participant.

Not everyone accepts his leap from mathematics to superintelligence. NYU professor Andrew Gordon Wilson argued that proving an existing conjecture is different from inventing new mathematical frameworks such as calculus or relativity.

“Nothing compares to proving the Riemann Hypothesis in terms of sheer intellectual might”. I disagree. The introduction of calculus, general relativity, and quantum mechanics, are more profound intellectual achievements. Creativity, taste, and intuition is the difference.

— Andrew Gordon Wilson (@andrewgwils) November 23, 2026

The Riemann result demonstrates a remarkable human-AI collaboration, but it does not prove that autonomous superintelligence exists.

Wang has urged the industry to change course while Meta continues developing the systems he fears could eventually exceed human oversight.

After testing countless pairs of running shorts over the years, the Hotty Hot High-Rise Lined Short from Lululemon is my fave for its sweat-wicking fabric and comfortable fit. The polyester blend wicks away sweat, prevents cling, and promotes airflow while running. The loose, flowy fit keeps me cool, while a built-in interior liner adds lightweight coverage and support without bulk.

The side pockets are small, but hold small essentials like a credit card, key, or energy gels for long runs. The leg openings are spacious, allowing for a full range of motion, and an adjustable drawstring secures the waistband for a customizable fit. Want to hit the road at the crack of dawn or at night? No sweat; reflective detailing improves visibility in dark or dim light, making early morning or evening runs safer.

I appreciate the 4-inch length, given I prefer more coverage, but a 2.5-inch length is available if you prefer a shorter fit. WH associate health and fitness editor Addison Aloian, NASM-CPT, is also a fan of the fit and vast color palette. “They never ride up or move around, which is hard to find in a running short,” she says. With tons of colors and sizes to choose from, you can't go wrong.

New Balance is a top brand in the running world, and the RC Short is one of my faves. It runs slightly big, but I love the extra breathing room during a sweat session.

The lightweight, flowy construction uses the brand’s quick-drying tech fabric (a polyester and spandex blend) to wick moisture from the skin. The breathable design promotes tons of airflow, creating a cooling effect while I run—especially ideal during scorching hot summer runs.

The seamless, interior lining reduces chafing and irritation, while the waistband features an adjustable drawstring to customize the fit. It’s also not too tight—some liners can feel like you’re wearing a diaper (hate). As for storage, there’s a back pocket for securing small running essentials and even tiny snacks like a granola bar when you’re on the move.

A pair of high cut shorts, such as the Alo Match Point Short, is a running staple. The high-cut at the thighs keeps things perfectly airy and flowy for optimal coolness when I get overheated, more so than the Lululemon Hotty Hot Short.

This construction, paired with its moisture-wicking polyester fabric, creates the perfect breathable running shorts. While it’s a bit short at just over two inches, there’s still great coverage with a built-in brief, and I find it doesn’t show too much skin.

WH style contributor Lily Wolhner also appreciates this loose style for various workouts. “My favorite part about this short is that it’s never clingy, so it doesn’t ride up the thigh or need constant re-adjusting while you’re working out,” Wolhner says. “I’ve worn it for months and recently tested it during a 45-minute strength and HIIT workout, as well as an hour-long cross-training workout—I never felt over-exposed or uncomfortable in it.”

By the looks of the elastic waistband, I expected it to dig into my skin—wrong. It felt comfortable, although it’s important to note this short does run big, so I suggest sizing down.

We love a two-for-one, and this short from Brooks is ideal for both trail running and running at the gym. It has light compression with a built-in tight liner that doesn’t sacrifice mobility.

The mega-durable polyester fabric resists tears and moisture, which makes it ideal for trail running in tough terrain. “I love the high waist, the zipper pocket to carry my keys, and the tight shorts under a looser short aesthetic,” Katz says.

Two waistband pockets are impressively large and can even fit a water flask, so you can always stay hydrated during your jogs.

I personally don’t love compression-lined shorts because I like to feel totally free, but if you prefer extra coverage and double layers, this short is ideal.

If you want a no-frills pair of shorts at an affordable price point that will stand the test of time, the Under Armour Play Up 3.0 belongs in your running gear collection. I’ve owned multiple pairs for years in eye-catching colors, and they’re still in good condition with no pills—even after dozens of runs and wash cycles.

The lightweight knit fabric made from smooth polyester has an anti-pill finish for extra durability, and is impressively comfy. Plus, it hides embarrassing sweat stains post-run, despite the slightly thicker material.

The waistband uses a wide elastic band that provides a secure fit without any adjustable features. However, I find it still fits roomy and allows for a full range of motion.

It includes deep side pockets but no enclosure, so I don’t recommend stashing anything super important besides fuel, like energy gels. I wear it the most for shorter, mid-distance runs and whenever I want to add a pop of color—it has 21 color options!

I usually don’t gravitate toward compression shorts since I don’t like feeling constricted, but the Athleta Salutation Stash 5-Inch Short offers the perfect amount of tightness. It hugs my thighs with gentle compression, while the high-rise waistband distributes pressure evenly for a secure fit without digging in. Plus, the two deep side pockets offer convenient storage for longer runs.

The smooth, double-knit fabric is buttery-soft and offers great coverage. While on the thicker side, it conceals sweat stains well—a huge win during long-haul runs. I wouldn’t say it feels the most breathable compared to other shorts in this guide, but the nylon and lycra blend wicks away sweat and dries fast.

Another huge selling point? The fabric’s UPF 50 protection, which prevents UV radiation from scorching your thighs. This is my favorite feature as someone fair-skinned and prone to nasty sunburns (IYKYK). Aside from its fabric, I love that it has a matching jacket for a coordinated workout set.

Tracksmith’s Van Cortlandt Shorts combine retro styling with a performance-driven design that makes them a winner both on and off the track. It’s made from a lightweight mesh fabric to maximize airflow, paired with an antimicrobial finish to help combat odor by wicking away sweat and limiting bacteria buildup during intense runs.

After summer runs when I’m dripping with sweat, I noticed zero smell—and that the short dries at the speed of light.

Like our best overall, it’s quite short at 2.5 inches, so if you prefer a longer style, you should look to other styles in this guide. On the flip side, it doesn’t disrupt my range of motion during speed work or long runs. As for fit, I found it runs true to size, but make sure to consult the size chart as always.

Running shorts with sweat-wicking fabric are the way to go, Katz says. Most shorts use a blend of polyester, spandex, and/or nylon, which lifts moisture from the skin while staying flexible during movement. Based on testing, it’s best to avoid cotton since it doesn’t dry nearly as fast and clings to the skin when wet.

It’s important to determine what kind of rise and inseam you desire. High-waisted running shorts offer more coverage and tummy control, while a mid-rise waist sits right at the hips. Ultimately, what you find most flattering for your body type is the best option.

The inseam is the length from the crotch to the bottom. A longer length will show less skin but may disrupt the range of motion, while some running shorts favorites, like the Lululemon Hotty Hot High-Rise Lined Short, offer a 2.5-inch option if you like a mini fit.

As for an interior liner or compression, this will make running shorts fit more snugly. “Compression is a matter of preference, but the goal in this material is to boost recovery,” says Katz. If you want a less constrictive fit, it’s probably best to avoid that feature.

In addition to my own testing, Women’s Health associate health and fitness editor Addison Aloian, NASM-CPT also extensively tested tons of running shorts to determine whether or not they’re the real deal. Each pair was worn during training runs or races for anywhere from three weeks to even three years to see how they performed and held up.

Essential features considered were materials, inseam, pockets, durability, and adjustability. Additionally, I asked a running coach for their go-to running shorts and guidance on how they should fit.
