#5013. Bitcoin ‘As Important as It’s Ever Been’ if Inflation Rises, Coinbase CEO Says

"Bitcoin investors tend to sell BTC when there's a big IPO. Then they come back."

That's Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong's take on Bitcoin investor behavior, less than a week after the record-breaking $93.5 billion IPO of Claude creator Anthropic.

"Historically, people rotate out of it to take advantage of a big IPO. Then they come back in," Armstrong wrote on X earlier today.

The limited window of opportunity to invest in an IPO helps explain the behavior Armstrong described. For an investor to buy at the IPO price, there's only a certain period during which they can request an allocation of shares. After that, the price is determined by the market.

On Nov. 19, Anthropic went public on the Nasdaq, and that brief window of opportunity mattered.

Shares were priced at $83, up from the $70-$78 range indicated just two days earlier. Anthropic's stock, trading under the ticker ANT, opened at $111.50.

If you bought at that opening price, you paid about 34% more per share than an investor who received an allocation at the IPO price.

When the IPO closed on Nov. 20, 1.127 billion shares had been sold, including 147 million additional shares purchased by underwriters exercising their option.

Of the $93.5 billion in gross proceeds, Anthropic itself received around $91.6 billion. The rest went to existing shareholders.

There was also a separate $26 billion private placement involving investors such as Microsoft, Nvidia, Google and others. In total, the combined transactions were valued at $119.5 billion.

As for the longer-term case for holding BTC, Armstrong's point concerns investors' expectations about the future purchasing power of their money.

"If you think there is going to be more inflation and money printing in the future, bitcoin is as important as ever."

At the heart of the matter is Bitcoin's 21 million supply limit.

If you expect governments to continue expanding the money supply, you may still be excited by the prospect of a major IPO. And you may sell some of your BTC to participate in it.

Armstrong's argument is that the window of opportunity to participate in a major IPO eventually closes.

However, the reasons investors bought Bitcoin in the first place may remain long after the newly listed stock starts trading.

#5011. South Korea wants banks to own more than 50% of domestic stablecoin issuers

South Korea’s stablecoin proposal gives banks majority control and establishes reserve-backed redemption protections for holders.

South Korea’s financial regulator proposed limiting initial domestic stablecoin issuance to licensed groups in which banks collectively own more than 50%.

Under the plan, a fintech or technology company could still hold the largest individual stake, as the Financial Services Commission (FSC) outlined on Nov. 24.

The legislative proposal calls stablecoins digital payment tokens and defines them as assets pegged to one currency and used mainly for payments. Issuers would put the tokens into circulation at an equivalent value in the underlying currency and would be barred from paying holders interest.

A domestic issuer would need an FSC license and at least 5 billion won in equity capital. Applicants would have to show they have the staff and facilities to operate, submit a viable business plan, and explain how they would prevent conflicts of interest.

Major shareholders and executives would also have to meet eligibility requirements.

The issuer would also need FSC approval for its issuance plan, including how many tokens it intended to issue, the maximum it could issue, how it would manage reserves, and how holders could redeem their tokens.

When a holder asked to redeem, the issuer would have to pay the equivalent value in currency without delay.

To meet those requests, issuers would keep reserves worth at least 100% of outstanding issuance with a reserve manager such as a bank. The proposal would shield the reserves from third-party seizure or setoff.

Under the proposed redemption rules, the institution managing the reserves could pay holders directly if the issuer went bankrupt, lost its license, or could no longer handle normal issuance and redemption after a disruption such as a hack.

The FSC says holders would have priority when the reserve manager makes those payments.

Overseas issuers would have a separate route to offer issuance and redemption in South Korea. An issuer would need adequate supervision in its home jurisdiction and a Korean branch with sufficient operating funds. It would have to register with the FSC and file separately for its foreign-issued tokens.

Platforms could only list tokens with the applicable approval or filing. The same requirement would apply to digital asset firms that trade, broker, or hold those tokens in custody.

The FSC said it would support deliberations in the National Assembly, while a later presidential decree would set detailed shareholder rules for domestic stablecoin issuers.

#5009. OpenAI Will Pay You Up to $8K to Preach the AI Gospel to Small Businesses

OpenAI Will Pay You Up to $8K to Preach the AI Gospel to Small Businesses

OpenAI wants people to spread the gospel of ChatGPT to their local businesses. And it is willing to pay them up to $8,000 a month to do it.

The company launched OpenWorks, a program that recruits AI-savvy individuals and small consulting teams to help neighborhood businesses figure out what to do with the technology. The idea is to move beyond telling a restaurant owner that AI will change everything and actually build something useful for the restaurant.

OpenAI will pay selected partners a monthly stipend of up to $8,000. In exchange, applicants must commit to four full days of free, in-person work with local businesses each month, plus one community workshop. It's not an $8,000 salary just for being good at prompts.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Anthropic with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

That said, this isn't a full-time job with an automatic $96,000 salary. The company advertises a maximum monthly stipend and asks partners to spend four full days each month providing free, in-person assistance, plus hosting one community workshop.

The application asks candidates to describe a real problem they've solved using AI, what changed afterward, and which businesses they'd help first. Knowing how to give ChatGPT clever instructions apparently isn't enough; experience in coding, automation, marketing or operations helps.

Small businesses pay nothing for the service. They pick a problem, work with a partner on a solution, and get three months of ChatGPT Business at no cost. OpenAI says the pilot covers independently owned U.S. businesses, but leaves out startups backed by venture capital, private-equity-owned companies, and software firms.

The company has some examples to sell the idea. In Fargo, North Dakota, the owners of Tiny Things, a gift shop selling miniatures, used ChatGPT with an OpenWorks partner to build an inventory dashboard. One owner estimated that commissioning a similar tool would have cost about $50,000.

In Charleston, a microgreens grower used the chatbot to find restaurants and write personalized pitches to chefs. He estimates his response rate went from 20% to 75% and says he landed 10 new restaurant customers in four months. Those are the businesses' own accounts, not independently audited results.

OpenWorks is starting in 20 communities, including New York, Chicago, Los Angeles, and Fargo. OpenAI is inviting applicants elsewhere, too, under the slogan "Help us reach every community in America."

The push comes as the company works to turn consumer enthusiasm into recurring business usage. As Decrypt reported in April, enterprise customers already accounted for more than 40% of OpenAI's revenue, according to the company.

Competition also provides an incentive. Anthropic overtook OpenAI in one measure of business AI adoption earlier this year, even as ChatGPT remained a major consumer destination.

Getting ChatGPT into more neighborhood businesses gives OpenAI another route to paying customers, though the company hasn't said what happens after the free three-month offer. It also follows an October effort with America's Small Business Development Centers to train advisers and reach at least 1,000 businesses through workshops.

OpenAI has not announced a general application deadline or a fixed stipend for everyone accepted. The form is open now, and its most important question is pretty straightforward: Can you actually show up four full days a month and help somebody run a business better?

#5007. CZ Urges 1Password Users to Change All Their Passwords

After a hacker stole customer data, Binance founder Changpeng Zhao advised 1Password users to change all the passwords stored in the service.

1Password offered different advice about what users should do after the incident was disclosed on Nov. 25. The password management service said hackers hadn't gained access to the passwords stored in users' vaults, so there was no need to reset them.

"If you use 1Password, recommend you to change ALL your passwords. It's a pain in the neck, but necessary," Zhao said on X, replying to a post from Coin Bureau about the breach.

If you have a crypto exchange login stored in 1Password, this distinction is important.

1Password says hackers could access the email address a customer uses to log in to the service. But they couldn't see the exchange password saved in the customer's vault.

Scammers could still use the stolen email addresses to contact people they know are 1Password users.

1Password started investigating on Nov. 19 after detecting signs of possible unauthorized access to an employee's corporate GitHub account.

From there, the hacker was able to steal private source code and inject malicious code into 1Password's backend services. The malicious code then downloaded certain administrative data about customers.

1Password publicly disclosed the breach on Nov. 25, six days later.

The company did not specify how many customers were affected or explain exactly how the hacker managed to take over the employee's account.

The stolen data included customer names, login email addresses, account and user IDs, and timestamps indicating account creation and last use.

The hacker also gained access to 1Password's software development and deployment systems.

1Password disabled the compromised employee's GitHub account and revoked the stolen access token.

The company also restored a clean version of the affected service and revoked or replaced potentially exposed internal credentials.

1Password also engaged independent security experts to review its response.

1Password recommends that customers check the 1Password app or type the company's website address directly into their browser if they receive an unexpected invitation or recovery message.

The company says it will never contact users to request their account password or Secret Key.

Update: 1Password claims that there is no need to change one's 1Password account password or any of the passwords saved in one's vault. No customer passwords were exposed in this incident.

Hi CZ! There’s no need to change your 1Password account password or any of the passwords you’ve saved in your vault. No customer passwords were exposed in this incident. We don’t store your account password or Secret Key, and getting into our backend systems didn’t give the attacker the keys to decrypt your vault. The attacker did copy account information for some customers, including names and email addresses, so we recommend watching for 1Password invitations or account recovery emails you weren’t expecting. You can read the full update on our blog: https://t.co/9fbzzAJr0B

Fidelity Investments has added AAVE, Chainlink (LINK) and Uniswap (UNI) to its Fidelity Crypto trading service, expanding its supported digital asset list from five to eight. The addition lifts the number of supported assets from five to eight and brings three DeFi tokens to eligible US customers.

Fidelity announced the update on its official website and in an X post. The platform now supports Bitcoin (BTC), Ethereum (ETH), Solana (SOL), Litecoin (LTC), AAVE, LINK, UNI and the Fidelity Digital Dollar (FIDD), a US dollar-pegged stablecoin the company announced in January 2026.

Each new token is tied to a different part of DeFi. AAVE is the token for Aave, a lending protocol that mediates cryptocurrency lending and borrowing.

UNI is the governance token for Uniswap, a decentralized exchange. LINK is used in Chainlink, an oracle network that delivers external information such as price data to smart contracts.

Trading and custody are handled by Fidelity Digital Assets, a subsidiary licensed as a U.S. National Trust Bank. The service is available to eligible U.S. customers aged 18 and over residing in states where Fidelity provides the service.

Fidelity launched Fidelity Crypto for individual investors in 2022, initially offering Bitcoin and Ether. The latest addition follows Charles Schwab’s November 9 listing of Solana, Avalanche and Chainlink on its spot crypto platform.

Fidelity’s addition of AAVE, UNI and LINK extends a major US brokerage’s retail crypto offering to DeFi infrastructure tokens. It also adds to competition among traditional brokerages for crypto-active customers, following Schwab’s recent expansion.

#5005. China's Z.ai Says Its New AI Model Can Think Like One Four Times Its Size

China's Z.ai Says Its New AI Model Can Think Like One Four Times Its Size

Chinese AI developer Z.ai released GLM-5.4 on Monday, introducing a new architecture that it claims delivers the reasoning capabilities of models nearly four times its size without requiring nearly as many parameters.

The Beijing-based company says its new 750-billion-parameter model can compete with systems containing two to three trillion parameters. It also supports a one-million-token context window, accepts images and video, and can generate up to 128,000 tokens in a single response, according to its technical documentation. Parameters are the internal values a model learns during training, while tokens are the chunks of text it processes and generates—roughly equivalent to words or parts of words.

The release comes as American companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google dominate the highest positions in AI performance rankings. Chinese developers, meanwhile, have increasingly focused on making powerful models cheaper to run, particularly for coding and autonomous agents.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Anthropic with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Z.ai has been among China's strongest competitors. As Decrypt reported in August, its predecessor GLM-5.3 was already competitive with leading American coding models, although it still trailed the best proprietary systems on several software engineering tests.

GLM-5.4 introduces what Z.ai calls a Loop Transformer, which processes information through the same 28 neural network layers twice. Traditional Transformers generally pass information through each layer once, so reusing layers effectively increases computational depth without increasing the number of stored parameters.

The company combines this approach with gated updates, which regulate how much information changes between passes, and a hybrid memory cache that avoids storing an entirely separate copy of previous calculations. Sparse attention also helps the model focus its computing power on relevant information rather than processing everything equally.

In controlled experiments on a smaller 30-billion-parameter model, Z.ai reported that its looping technique increased accuracy on AIME 2025, a mathematics examination benchmark scored by the percentage of correctly solved problems, from 19.17% to 30.42%.

GPQA Diamond, a graduate-level science question-answering test also scored by correct-answer percentage, improved from 47.58% to 56.26%. The experiments required approximately 10% additional training compute, while reducing generated reasoning tokens by 10% to 14% on several tests.

Those results concern the experimental architecture, not independently established performance for GLM-5.4 itself. Z.ai has not published a comprehensive flagship benchmark comparison demonstrating that the new model matches Claude or GPT.

The company is also promoting what it calls Generalized Coding: using programming to accomplish tasks beyond software development. Its demonstrations include building a video game, creating 3D environments, and designing a six-axis robotic arm using engineering software.

The company's previous flagship costs $1.40 per million input tokens and $4.40 per million output tokens through its API. By comparison, OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Sol costs $2 and $10, while Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 costs $4 and $20, respectively.

At those published rates, GLM-5.3 is considerably cheaper than its American counterparts, although GLM-5.4's own API pricing has not been announced. Its actual performance-per-dollar advantage therefore cannot yet be calculated.

China has other serious contenders. Alibaba's Qwen 4 Max recently topped Chinese competitors on Arena's agent leaderboard, while Moonshot's Kimi K3 and DeepSeek V4 have challenged American developers on coding performance and API pricing.

The performance gap remains contested. A U.S. government evaluation placed DeepSeek roughly eight months behind the American frontier, although researchers questioned its methodology.

Z.ai itself remains on the U.S. Commerce Department's Entity List, following its January 2025 designation over concerns that its AI research could support Chinese military modernization. The restrictions limit access to controlled American technology, but have not stopped the company from releasing new models.

#5004. Your Guide to Running on the Treadmill This Winter

Here’s why it feels harder to run indoors—and how to hack it to make it more enjoyable.

There’s almost no other cardio machine that brings up as many feelings as the treadmill. For the first few years of my running career, I’d do just about everything I could to avoid hopping on one, even if that meant running in freezing temps or heavy rain.

Then, last winter happened. There was more snow and ice on the ground in New York City than I had seen in a long time, but I had a half-marathon to train for. It left me no choice: I had to move my workouts to the treadmill unless I wanted to end up like that meme where the woman says snow is the perfect texture for running just to wipe out on live television a few seconds later.

But, as any treadmill hater knows, moving a run indoors isn’t as simple as it sounds. A lot changes on a tread—form, mental stimulation, pace—and it can totally mess with your head. Once you understand why, though, it’s a lot easier to work with the treadmill instead of against it; here’s how.

Because it is! For starters, your form changes. “Many people shorten their stride on the treadmill—me included,” says Amy Woods, a USAT-certified run coach and ISSA-certified strength and conditioning coach. “We also tend to run a little more upright.”

There’s a simple reason behind it. When you’re running outside, your legs have all the space they need for each stride, but on a treadmill, you’re contained to the length and width of the belt. Plus, most people tend to stick too close to the front of the tread, making their space even smaller, says Morgan Mowers, PT, DPT, a physical therapist and V.02-certified run coach.

Between a shortened stride and the fact that it’s a bit easier to propel yourself forward when you’ve got the help of the moving belt, you end up using different muscles on a treadmill compared to outdoors. “We see a decrease in activation of hamstrings and glutes, those bigger propellers that push you forward,” Mowers says. Instead, you’re seeing more activation in your hip flexors, quads, calves, and knees.

On paper, a lot of these differences should actually make treadmill running easier than running outside. Another example? A treadmill provides a consistent surface. Outside, terrain and incline can vary with each step, so you call on more stabilizing muscles in your ankles and calves, Mowers says. “With every step, there's a little bit of a change when you're running outside versus on a treadmill,” she says. “Even if you are changing up the incline, it's the same exact surface over and over again.” You also don’t have to deal with the same environmental challenges—like heat and wind resistance—that come with running outside. There’s even a famous 1996 study that claims runners should set their incline to 1 percent to accommodate for the difference.

Even with all these easier-sounding differences, running on a treadmill often feels anything but. For many people, myself included, slowing down on a treadmill is the norm. One possible reason: You may just not be used to it, Woods says. Running safely on a treadmill, especially at higher speeds, takes practice. “It's definitely a different feeling when you're running on a treadmill,” Woods says. “You have to be more aware of your foot placement, your arm swing, and where your eyes are looking.” Even if you’re not consciously aware of it, your proprioception (your ability to sense your body’s position in space) could be affected.

Plus, when you’re on the treadmill, you’re stuck at one pace unless you change it, Mowers points out. “That consistency that your body is feeling on a treadmill can make it feel harder, and also may result in you going at an overall slower pace,” she says. When you hop on a treadmill, you start yourself at a pace and settle in until you physically change it. Over the course of a mile outdoors, in comparison, you may start at an 11:00 pace, then speed up to a 10:45 pace for most of it, and end up cruising at a 10:30 pace—all without really noticing. Even though your effort feels the same, your outdoor mile ends up faster.

Then there’s the mental side of things. Outside, you’ve got much more stimulation, says Rachelle Reed, PhD, an exercise physiologist. Your surroundings can offer the perfect distraction, and the natural variations in scenery, incline, terrain, and pace can help keep your brain more engaged too. This can have an impact on your rate of perceived exertion (RPE), Reed says. In fact, a 2019 meta-analysis found that at faster speeds, runners rated their effort as harder on a treadmill compared to outdoors. Basically, it’s harder to go hard on the tread. And because running on a treadmill is technically easier than running outdoors because you have less variation, wind resistance, and environmental factors to navigate at any given moment, that higher RPE really speaks to the mental effects of being inside, Reed says.

The good news? All these differences between treadmill and outdoor running only really matter if you’re training for a race. That’s because come race day, you’ll want your muscles fully prepped to accommodate your outdoor stride, along with the ability to run across inconsistent terrain and in various elements, Mowers says. Meanwhile, if you’re just looking to do cardio, you can take your pick between the two.

If you are in fact training for a race, how should a treadmill fit into your training? In this case, going outside tends to be superior to staying in, our experts agree. Don’t move your run to the tread at just any sign of inconvenience—running in the rain, cold, and (reasonable) heat all make you a better runner, and you never know if those conditions will pop up on race day, so you’ll be glad to have the practice.

Still, there are definitely situations where it’s not a good idea to go outside. Mowers draws the line when it comes to safety: If the ground is icy, snowy, or slippery in any way, she’ll stay inside to avoid potential injury. If temps are dangerously hot, she’ll run on the treadmill. If there’s risk from serious weather, like thunder and lightning or flooding, she’ll also stay safe indoors. And, she’ll stick to her tread in the event of poor air quality (anything that’s an air quality index over 101).

It’s always worth considering personal safety, too. If your only window to run is late at night and you feel more comfortable staying indoors, do that.

How hot is too hot? This is going to vary down to the person and place. Anything above 85 degrees can be dangerous, Woods says, and you also need to factor in dew point, humidity, and the effort of your run. (Harder efforts are more risky than easier ones.) If temps are higher and you decide to run outdoors, make sure you bring plenty of hydration and fuel, go slower than normal, and pay attention to signs of overheating.

There’s also the convenience factor. You may need to do a run on the treadmill because it’s more accommodating to your schedule or childcare needs. That’s totally okay too. Ideally, the majority of your runs (we’re talking about 80 percent, and especially your long runs) will be outside, but if you’re someone who finds themselves needing to do the bulk of their running indoors, a run coach can help you make sure you’re prepped for race day. (Woods works with athletes who do the bulk of their training on treads—it’s possible!) The treadmill exists for a reason, and your training will not be affected by the occasional indoor run.

First and foremost, don’t be too hard on yourself about pace. “I always disconnect from pace on the treadmill,” Woods says. Instead, she focuses on her time and RPE. It’s really about thinking about the “spirit of the workout,” she says. For example, you can pay attention to what heart rate zone or effort level you’re supposed to get to and match that—even if that looks slower and feels harder indoors.

And, no, you don’t need to set your incline to 1 percent to compensate for bringing your workout indoors, our experts agree. The biggest reason? The study that established the idea was very small (it had just nine participants) and done only in men. That said, the incline buttons will become useful depending on the kind of run you have on deck for the day.

Finally, give yourself a good warm-up on the treadmill, Mowers says. “Just the act of getting on a treadmill is going to increase our heart rate a little bit because we're a hamster on a wheel; we're trying not to fall off of this thing, and we're so aware of the fact that we're running,” she says. You may need at least 10 to 15 minutes to settle in before getting started with the rest of your workout.

Here’s how to approach different kinds of runs indoors.

Nothing really has to change, Woods says. It may take you a little longer to run a 5K on your treadmill, but try to stick to the appropriate lower heart rate zones and RPE that you’d normally achieve on these kinds of runs outdoors.

You can play with incline if you’d like—but it’s not a requirement if this is a one-off run you’re doing inside. Running for one day on a completely flat surface won’t affect your training. One reason you may want to try changing the incline may simply be because it adds some variety and stimulation, Woods says. If you’re someone who struggles because the treadmill feels boring, try increasing the incline anywhere from 1 to 4 percent for anywhere from 30 seconds to a few minutes every so often.

Another hack: Every 10 minutes, increase your speed slightly. That should give you enough time to warm up a little each time and settle into the pace, so you shouldn’t see much of a jump in demand on your heart rate or effort.

This one gets a bit trickier, Woods says. Going at all-out speeds on a treadmill can be much tougher—and not feel super safe. This is a time when you’ll want to think about the spirit of the workout. If you have intervals where you’re supposed to get to max heart rate efforts, instead of turning up the speed super high, you can increase the incline in addition to adjusting the speed slightly, Woods says. That should still get you to your zone 4 or 5, all while allowing you to stay slower and feel more in control. This is much easier to accomplish in a tempo run (where you’re holding the pace for longer chunks of time) compared to intervals, so you could also swap an interval run for tempo too.

You also have the option to skip a speed workout, Woods says. Missing one session won’t have an impact on your training, and if you’d rather not do it on the treadmill, you also have the option to switch it with another run for the week.

Now, here’s a workout that translates pretty well to the treadmill: All you have to do is up your incline for the duration marked in your workout. Woods recommends sticking between 1 and 4 percent as a good rule of thumb, but you can always bump up to 5 to 8 as long as you can keep good run form.

Ideally, you can move your long run to another day when you can run outside. But, if not, go by time—not mileage. Woods doesn’t recommend running on a treadmill for longer than two hours unless you are very experienced on one because of how it affects your form.

You also have the option to break up your run and do 90 minutes in the morning and 90 minutes in the afternoon. “This will help with form deterioration which is more noticeable and can be more dangerous on a tread,” Woods says.

While you’re on your long run, you’ll also want to incorporate moments of incline running and even some pace variation—both for improving your running and also giving yourself a mental reset. Woods also loves to sprinkle in 15- to 30-second walking breaks every mile or so to reset her form and hydrate.

Then the world is really your oyster on the treadmill, but all the same ideas apply: Focus on time and effort, not pace. And, feel free to sprinkle in different inclines and speeds to work different heart rate zones and find moments of mental reset.

#5003. Australian Crypto Investors Turn to Loans Ahead of 2027 Tax Reform

Home » Crypto Market News » Australian Crypto Investors Turn to Loans Ahead of 2027 Tax Reform

Upcoming capital gains tax reforms are prompting crypto holders to reconsider how they access cash without selling their digital assets

One in five Australian cryptocurrency investors would consider borrowing against their digital assets rather than selling them, as upcoming tax changes push holders to rethink their financial strategies.

A survey commissioned by digital asset wealth platform Nexo found that 22.7% of Australian crypto holders would consider borrowing against their holdings instead of selling, compared with 10% of other investors.

The findings come as Australia prepares to overhaul its capital gains tax (CGT) system from July 1, 2027.

Nexo surveyed 1,000 Australian investors this October to examine how major expenses and rising living costs affect investment decisions.

The results suggest that crypto holders are more inclined to avoid selling their investments when they need additional funds.

Beyond the 22.7% considering borrowing, another 19.7% said they had delayed or decided against selling their crypto holdings.

Crypto investors can borrow against their existing holdings instead of selling them for cash. This allows them to access money while keeping their Bitcoin or other digital assets, and potentially benefit if their value increases.

The trend comes against a broader backdrop of financial pressure. According to the survey, 29.4% of all investors had delayed, reduced or cancelled a major purchase or financial plan over the previous 12 months.

The upcoming CGT reform is another factor investors may need to consider.

Under Australia’s current system, eligible individuals, trusts and partnerships can receive a 50% capital gains tax discount on assets held for more than 12 months.

From July 1, 2027, this discount will be replaced by cost base indexation and a 30% minimum tax on eligible gains.

Under transitional arrangements, gains accrued before that date will remain eligible for the existing 50% discount, while gains accumulated afterward will be subject to the new rules.

Crypto ownership in Australia is at a record high, with 2.79 million Australians holding or trading cryptocurrency, according to the figures cited in an Australian investor Study.

That equals about 24% of the country’s 11.5 million investors, up from roughly 15% in 2023, making crypto as widely held as exchange-traded funds (ETFs).

As ownership expands, the demand for financial products that allow investors to access liquidity without selling their holdings could also increase.

Consequently, as their holdings rise in value, more investors may look for ways to cover major expenses without selling their crypto.

The new CGT rules could make some investors think twice before selling crypto that has increased in value. As a result, more holders may consider borrowing against their holdings to cover major expenses without having to sell their assets and potentially trigger a capital gains tax bill.

#5002. The 8 Best Standing Desks for Walking Pads, Tested and Reviewed

From budget picks to tricked-out options for a better WFH space.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

You log a lot of time at your desk, making it fair to wonder how to create a workspace that’s as comfortable and healthy for you as possible. If sitting on your butt all day isn’t your idea of a good time, it makes sense to consider investing in a walking pad. To create a seamless workspace, you’ll need a special desk to go with that. The best standing desks for walking pads allow you to cruise along as you work, while still providing all the usual trappings you expect from a desk.

While TikTok is packed with happy-looking people working this way, the treadmill desk is more than a trend. Research ties sitting all day with a higher risk of developing back pain and even issues with cardiovascular health, making it a good idea to try to get up and move as much as possible during your day.

“Prolonged sitting has been linked to a number of health concerns, which is why many people are turning to standing desks,” says Andrew J. Bach, DO, a physiatrist at Cedars-Sinai Spine Center in Los Angeles “A standing desk allows you to get your usual computer-based work done while on your feet, and it comes with several benefits over sitting all day.” (He lists off better circulation, less strain on your back, more calories burned, and better digestion as just a few.)

But proper form is critical with these. “People should keep in mind how long they have been in a certain position, and their posture specifically,” says Meg Darmofal, DPT, a physical therapist at Michigan State University. You don’t want to shrug your shoulders, reach too far forward, bend over, or crane your neck up or down to see your screen, she says—all of those can put you at risk for developing aches and pains.

To find the best standing desks for walking pads, we consulted experts and had Women's Health editors test several popular models in their own workspaces. Our top pick is the Uplift Standing Desk V3, thanks to its easy height adjustments, customizable design, and compatibility with a walking pad. Ahead, find our favorite options for different budgets, spaces, and work-from-home setups.

While everyone has different needs in a standing desk, the Uplift V3 is packed with enough features and adjustability to make it a good fit for most. This motorized desk has a height range of 22.6 to 48.7 inches and comes in a wide range of tabletop widths and desktop styles, giving you plenty to choose from.

The desk has an impressive 355-pound lifting capacity, so you can pile a lot on it. WH copyeditor Deanna Martin tested the V3 alongside a walking pad and loved how easily the setup transformed her home office. The desk moves up and down with the touch of a keypad, making it easy to switch between sitting, standing, and walking throughout the workday.

Martin also liked the customizable accessories, which include storage options and even a hammock. There's also a companion app that tracks your standing progress and estimated calorie burn, though you'll need a Bluetooth adapter to connect it to the desk. Best of all, she found the entire setup super easy to assemble.

At over $600, the V3 is certainly an investment. But its versatile design, smooth height adjustments, and 15-year warranty are worth the price point.

It’s fair to expect to pay more for a motorized standing desk, but this Flexispot option manages to deliver that important feature with a relatively low price tag. The desk moves between 28 and 47.6 inches, giving you plenty to work with. It also has four height presets operated by an LED control panel, and a relatively roomy desktop space.

The desk includes a hook for your headphones or bag, allowing you to keep them in close reach while you work. It also can handle 176 pounds of weight, which should be plenty to work with. While it doesn’t have as many features as pricier desks like the Uplift 3, it’s still a solid, sturdy option to support you through your workday and comes much more affordably.

Whether you already have a desk you like or just don’t want to splash out for a totally new model, a standing desk converter can be a good middle ground. This option from Rocelco simply plops on top of your existing table to create a standing desk, so you can use a walking pad without replacing your entire WFH setup.

While some standing desk converters are small, this one can hold up to two large monitors, a laptop, and more. There’s a retractable keyboard tray, although it may not extend far enough for everyone's needs. The height adjustment is manual, but easy to do with the turn of a dial. There’s even a grommet hole to help you organize your cords, giving you a lot of the perks of a standing desk without the full commitment. Just make sure your existing desk and converter are tall enough to accommodate your walking pad.

A contoured standing desk allows you to get in close to your workspace, with an ergonomic design that can help you maintain a comfortable position while walking on a treadmill. This Fully Jarvis desk is sleek and comfortable, with a gently sloping and curved front that feels natural under your arms.

During testing, we were able to put this desk together quickly. It has a very sturdy feel, which is helpful when you’re walking while using it. The desk also thoughtfully includes an outlet and USB/lightning charger, so you can plug in your computer without having to bend over. The motor adjusts easily, although it can be a little choppy when you move up and down. Overall, we found that it was easy and comfortable to use. It looks and feels like a high-quality desk thanks to its bamboo surface and sturdy steel frame, making this a workspace you’ll use for years.

Having a little extra storage space can go a long way when you're trying to keep your home office organized. This Sanodesk standing desk features built-in drawers to stash away your office clutter. It's also motorized, so you can easily adjust the height when you want to sit, stand, or hop on your walking pad.

WH Designer Taryn Colbert tested the desk for two weeks and gave it a four out of five. She liked its spacious, easy-to-clean surface and preset heights. “It’s perfect,” she says, adding that it was “easy to put together for a person thats not very handy.”

Her biggest gripes? She wished the power plug were positioned farther toward the back of the desk, rather than toward the front and side, and would have preferred a long, slim drawer for additional storage.

This electric standing desk from Veken has a compact design that won't take over your home office, along with a motorized height adjustment system that makes it easy to switch between sitting and standing. There are also programmable height presets, so you don't have to find your preferred position every time.

WH Fitness Editor Cori Ritchey tested the desk for two to four weeks and gave it a five out of five. She was super impressed by how sturdy it felt, even when raised to its maximum height. “It feels well made for a desk that the buyer assembles (no shaky IKEA feeling here, even when at its max height!),” she says. Ritchey also liked the easy-to-use height adjustments and wide range of positions.

Her biggest gripe was the size. While the 36-inch desktop was great for occasional use, she wished she'd gone up a size for everyday work. She also found the textured surface a little tricky to clean after spills.

This walking pad features a removable desktop that attaches to the treadmill's railings, giving you a convenient spot for your laptop or tablet while you clock your steps. WH Lifestyle Director Lindsay Geller tested the setup for over a month and gave it a five out of five. She especially liked how sturdy the desktop felt once attached and how easy it was to remove. “This is a really great way to get a second desk without actually committing to buying a full desk,” she says, noting that she shares a home office with her husband. She also found assembly straightforward, putting the entire setup together by herself in about an hour.

The desk is admittedly basic, and the treadmill doesn't offer adjustable incline. Geller also found the walking surface a little narrow for jogging, making this a better option for walking while working than more intense workouts.

Every standing desk has either a set height or height range. Bach points out that height is a “key factor” in your desk. “If you’re especially tall or short, make sure the desk can adjust to a level that works for you,” he says. Just keep in mind that you’ll want to include the height of your walking pad when figuring out the right standing desk height for you, since you’ll be on top of it while you use your desk. “Returning a bulky standing desk can be a hassle, so it’s best to get the right fit from the start,” Bach says. Ideally, your desk should be high enough that you can type comfortably while standing on your walking pad, without having to hunch over or raise your shoulders.

Not all standing desks are adjustable, but many are—and it’s a nice feature to have. “Being able to easily lower and raise the desk is important because, in some scenarios, returning to sitting is good as well,” Darmofal says. Some desks can be heavy and awkward to move manually, which can be frustrating if you plan to switch between sitting and standing during the day, Bach says. “Motorized options are the most convenient, since they transition with the push of a button,” he adds. (Just keep in mind that motorized options tend to cost more.)

At the end of the day, this is still a desk, and you need one that will hold your stuff. Make sure you factor in space to hold your computer, pens, notepad, water bottle, and anything else you usually have on your desk. If you're using a walking pad, you'll also want enough room for your keyboard and monitor so you don't have to lean forward while walking.

It’s important to make sure that your desk’s legs and any footing are wide enough to leave space for your walking pad to slip between. Pay close attention to the walking pad dimensions and desk dimensions, leaving a little room around the pad so you’re not jamming it in there.

We should also note that a lot of our standing desk selections below don't come with a walking pad (though the Sharper Image Treadmill Desk is an all-in-one option), meaning it's an additional expense. If you don't already have one, make sure to check out our under-desk treadmill buying guide.

I consulted with Bach and Darmofal to help identify what to look for in standing desks for walking pads. From there, I researched top models, narrowing the field based on criteria like comfort, adjustability, and ease of use. Because everyone has a different experience, I also paid close attention to customer reviews and prioritized desks with overwhelmingly positive feedback.

From there, Women's Health editors put several standing desks to the test in their own workspaces. Our testers included Cori Ritchey, Lindsay Geller, Taryn Colbert, and Deanna Martin, who evaluated the desks for build quality, ease of assembly, adjustability, size, and overall functionality. Testing periods ranged from one week to over a month, with editors using their desks while sitting, standing, or walking on an under-desk treadmill. #5001. Trump Says He 'Made the Deal' to Reinstate Jensen Huang, Sparking Bipartisan Backlash

Trump Says He 'Made the Deal' to Reinstate Jensen Huang, Sparking Bipartisan Backlash

U.S. President Donald Trump has taken credit for Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia, drawing criticism from lawmakers in both parties who say the administration has yet to explain what assurances it gave the company's board.

"I convinced them," Trump told CNBC in a phone interview on Monday, shortly after Nvidia reinstated Huang as president and CEO. "I made the deal."

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Nvidia with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Trump said the board had asked for assurances that Huang was not a national security threat, and that the administration provided them based on "everything we know." He said a government investigation had found that Huang himself was exonerated. Asked whether last week's stock losses had shaped his view, Trump said "probably so."

The board's decision was sealed by a personal promise from Trump on Sunday, CNBC reported, citing three people familiar with its thinking. Senior administration officials had contacted directors overnight on Friday, and Huang then joined meetings with the board over the weekend, the outlet said. The board's statement cited input from "senior levels of the United States government" without naming anyone.

Attorney General Todd Blanche told Trump and Vice President JD Vance on Saturday that Huang was not the target or subject of any Justice Department investigation, and that there was no evidence he had broken laws, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing U.S. officials.

During a marathon board session on Sunday, Huang disclosed additional affairs beyond the two that had been widely reported, but was contrite, the newspaper said, citing people familiar with the discussion.

Trump told The New York Times that he had consulted Blanche and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton before recommending Huang's return. "I had to go to them before I recommended this," he said. A day earlier, Clayton had said that the U.S. investigation into Alice Huang and her former company, Megaspeed, was ongoing.

The reversal came six days after board chair Harvey Jones said directors did not intend to bring Huang back. Trump later posted an AI-generated image on Truth Social showing Huang holding a red bra aloft in his raised fist, in a pose modeled on the photo of Trump after the 2024 assassination attempt on his life.

Huang's reinstatement drew the ire of lawmakers on both sides of the aisle.

"The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company's board still owe Congress answers," Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), ranking member of the Senate Banking Committee, said in a statement. She called on the administration to explain what input was given, and by which officials.

Republicans also pushed back. Sen. Tom Cotton (R-AR), chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, tweeted that the controversy over Nvidia and Megaspeed was "not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back," and pledged to pass chip export-control bills including his Chip Security Act.

I have warned the administration from the start about Communist China obtaining our most advanced chips through both smuggling and remote access. The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it’s not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back.…

— Tom Cotton (@SenTomCotton) November 23, 2026

"No national security risk? Based on what?" Sen. John Cornyn (R-TX) tweeted, quoting the board's statement. Sen. John Curtis (R-UT) asked who in government had weighed in and what they told the board, noting that it had ruled out Huang's return only a week earlier. "I'd like to know what changed," he wrote.

Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-NE) tweeted that Huang's behavior "does not support reinstatement," adding that Nvidia still had to answer for national security concerns and "unaccounted-for chips."

Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY), who is expected to become House Speaker in January, called the board's decision "indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible" in a statement. He promised an investigation into Nvidia and into what he called "corrupt abuse of power" by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and his department.

Trump's own Nvidia holdings may have gained as much as $15 million in value on Monday, according to the Financial Times, which calculated that he could have held up to 370,000 shares as of September 30, based on his latest ethics disclosure. At the low end of the disclosure's ranges, he would have held about 32,000 shares and gained $1.3 million. The White House did not respond to the newspaper's request for comment.

Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-AZ) tweeted that the president was "selling out our national security to keep the stock market high," calling for an investigation into stock trades made before the announcement.

Nvidia shares closed up 31.5% at $165.05 on Monday, adding about $950 billion to its market value, before slipping 5% to $156.82 in premarket trading on Tuesday, according to Yahoo! Finance.

Huang is due to sit for a closed-door interview with three House committees on December 1, and to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on December 3. On Monday, the Commerce Department also added Megaspeed to its Entity List trade blacklist.

#4998. Raving in Your 40s, 50s, and 60s? These Women Say It’s the Best Self-Care They’ve Found

Why women are turning to the EDM scene in the name of mental health.

Ask Karen Manson, 65, how she likes to recharge, and she’ll tell you this: a night of pounding bass, a sweaty dance floor, and getting home in the wee hours of the morning. She’s loved music her whole life and was always drawn to EDM, but marrying and having kids young left little room to explore it. Then, three years ago, her husband died, and she began thinking about how short and precious life is—and decided it was time to push herself to try new experiences.

That’s how she ended up at her first rave last year, solo. She was nervous, but spent the night dancing, and left with new friends and a newfound confidence. “I felt uninhibited,” she says. She’s attended more than 20 raves since.

Manson isn’t an outlier. Midlife women are prioritizing their mental health now more than ever, according to a 2026 study in the journal Women’s Health that analyzed nearly 1,000 surveys about women’s health priorities and concerns. And a number of them are finding relief on the dance floor.

A 2025 study in Psychology of Music surveyed 136 women ages 40 to 65 about why they’re involved in EDM experiences. The overwhelming response was that raving was a meaningful part of their mental well-being—an outlet for stress, a source of connection, and a rare place to escape the demands of everyday life, according to the survey.

“There is a rise in older people attending electronic dance music events, raves, clubs, parties, festivals,” says Alice O’Grady, PhD, a professor of applied performance at the University of Leeds, who co-authored the Psychology of Music study. “The motivations for women going are pretty much characterized as the same as they are for any age: the love of the music, the ability to socialize with existing friends, the atmosphere of the environment, and the sense of community.” Put simply: These music events are plain fun.

The EDM scene is no longer the epitome of youth culture, O’Grady adds, and it’s become more socially acceptable for women to embrace this genre of joy as they get older. That shift may reflect changing attitudes about aging, with women potentially feeling less constrained by traditional expectations about how they’re “supposed” to spend their time as they age. Social media has also made it much easier to discover niche music scenes, while a growing focus on mental health, movement, pleasure, and community may be encouraging women to seek out experiences that just make them feel good.

The older you get, the harder it can be to find a place where you can be playful, spontaneous, and fully present with other people. For some, the rave scene provides exactly that. “You've got more responsibility, more commitments,” O’Grady says. “You want that escape, you want that ability to connect through music and immerse yourself in an environment that allows you to be expressive and just shake off some of those roles that older women carry.”

Samantha Hillery, 43, started raving in her 20s as a way to let loose and have fun. But as life got busier with work, family, and kids, she stopped going. Years later, while searching for fun things to do in her area with friends, she came across Bingo Loco, a high-energy party with EDM, dancing, confetti, and—yes—bingo, and found her way back to it.

Now, Hillery gives herself permission to step away from the endless list of adult responsibilities. “As we get older and super busy with our lives, we forget how fun we maybe used to be, and it seems like something that was so far in the past,” she says. “But when you’re able to go out and rave surrounded by a bunch of friends and people that just want to have a good time, you remember that part of you isn’t lost.”

For some, keeping up with friends also becomes more challenging as you age and enter new eras of your life. Social obligations often come second, competing with work schedules, children, relationships, and other obligations, says Madison Liddle, LMHC, a licensed psychotherapist at Madison Liddle Therapy and co-founder of The Practice Co, a co-working space for therapists. At a music event like these, though, spontaneous connection is built into the experience.

Hundreds or thousands are gathered around the same music, moving to the same rhythm, creating an immediate sense of belonging. It’s a concept called collective effervescence, which is “a feeling of joy and connection when a group of people are in a shared space doing a shared thing,” Liddle explains. “Social connection is a really strong determinant of health as we age, and raving offers an opportunity to create and be in community with people with shared interests.”

Getting out and meeting new people is the main reason Manson is so attracted to rave culture—she’s found the crowds to be welcoming and friendly. “Life can become quite small if you don't push yourself,” she says, alluding to feeling alone after her husband’s passing. “I enjoy meeting people, I enjoy conversations. I'm not good at home in my own company—I need socialization.” Dancing with new friends is the way to do that, and it keeps her feeling energized.

In fact, in Manson’s experience, the EDM scene has seemed remarkably friendly to people of all ages and backgrounds. O’Grady agrees: “Women need spaces that are inclusive, welcoming, and accessible, and the rave scene actually does that quite well,” says O’Grady. You’ll feel a sense of belonging, like you’re part of something bigger than yourself, even if you’re there alone, she adds. The music creates an instant common language, while dancing alongside friends and strangers turns what could be an individual activity into something meaningful and collective.

The physical perks of dancing are well documented. It strengthens the cardiovascular, metabolic, musculoskeletal, and cognitive systems, as WH previously reported. It can also improve coordination, balance, and stability, which becomes especially important with age. But it can boost your mental health too, mainly because it helps you stay present. When you’re fully focused on what you’re hearing, feeling, and doing, there’s less room to get caught up in the mental replaying and worrying that can fuel stress, Liddle says.

In fact, many participants in the Psychology of Music study described dancing at raves as a way to ease anxiety, depression, and low moods, says co-author Alinka Greasley, PhD, a professor of music psychology at the University of Leeds. Anxiety can keep the mind focused on what might go wrong, while depression can make the present feel flat.

Raving, by contrast, demands attention in a different way. Instead of sitting with your thoughts, you’re listening to loud, immersive music, dancing to the beat, and anticipating the next drop, Liddle explains. That physical engagement helps interrupt rumination and creates a sense of clarity that lasts beyond the dance floor; it can help clear your head.

Alex Daly attended her first EDM show at 40 after her partner, who’d been going to raves for years, encouraged her to come along. A year later, raving has become a central part of her wellness routine. If she’s having a stressful week and doesn’t have an EDM show on her calendar, she immediately starts looking for one. “Once I’m in the crowd, I get into a flow state, and moving my body to the beat really helps me process my emotions,” says Daly, now 41. “Dancing helps me stop ruminating, get out of my head, and back into my body.” For a few hours, there’s simply less room for the mental noise of everyday life. In a way, it’s like the pounding beat is a reset button you can dance to.

Of course, rave culture has long been tied to recreational drugs like MDMA, which can bring on feelings of euphoria, connection, and stress relief. That link hasn’t disappeared. Some of the women in the Psychology of Music study said they took drugs, often to keep their energy up for dancing, while others went purely for the music and the movement.

However, drugs weren’t what gave the women a sense of belonging, the study uncovered. “That's very much already there from their perspective,” Greasley says. “The drugs are more to do with [increasing] energy levels and also the marrying of the drugs and the music. Many women called it a spiritual experience to be in ecstatic states whilst dancing to the music.”

Karen D., 62, who asked that her last name be withheld because she discusses her drug use, sees it the same way. She started going to raves in her early 50s with her second husband. While she partakes in recreational drug use, she also knows people who attend raves completely sober. For her, the bonding comes from dancing with like-minded people who are all just happy to be there.

But Karen acknowledges that drugs heighten those feelings and add to the mental health boost she gets from raving. “I feel like my brain’s reconnecting in ways that it has forgotten how to connect,” she says. “I can get down with what’s going on in my life at times, and it completely transforms me into a much more positive person.”

Wellness advice in your 40s, 50s, and beyond is often the same advice over and over: protect your sleep, drink less, manage stress, and stick to a routine. But in contrast, this group of ravers finds genuine self-care in the act of staying out late, dancing for hours, and disrupting those prescribed wellness rules. “In this world where everything is so optimized and planned and scheduled, there is something that we lose in terms of fun,” says Liddle, noting that raving brings it to the forefront. The key is to accept the occasional trade-off—less sleep in the name of mental health benefits—and to strike a balance between partying and recovering.

Manson has attended a couple of Daybreaker events, which are morning, sober parties and raves, often starting around 6 a.m. Early parties like these are becoming more common. O’Grady adds that more women DJs are putting on earlier shows with the attitude of: “We all want to get together, we all want to have a dance, but we want to be in bed by midnight.”

However, Manson prefers later shows because she finds that’s when more traditional EDM is played. But staying up until 4 a.m. at these events has been a bit of a learning curve, so she tries to limit her events to one per weekend. “The enthusiasm's there, but I'm not prepared to spend so much time recovering,” she says. “Once is great, it does what I want it to do. It makes me feel good. I get to connect with people that I enjoy spending time with.” She prioritizes sleeping in the next morning, and just rests the next day if she needs to. Then, she can still go to the gym and take long walks during the week. (She doesn’t work anymore, so she has more flexibility to rest.)

Despite the missed-out-on sleep, Karen D. finds that rave life rejuvenates her. “If I've been away at a festival for a weekend, I come back very tired because I need more sleep,” she says. “However, I do feel refreshed somehow—more clearheaded.”

But she still makes sure to still get seven hours of sleep if she goes to bed late, so then she can still fulfill her responsibilities at home, like taking her grandson to school. The tradeoff is also worth it for her, and in fact, going to raves inadvertently benefits her wellness routine. It “really helps motivate me to do weight training, to go running, to do all these wholesome recognized exercises, because I want to stay well to be able to go and dance [until] 3 o'clock in the morning,” she says.

Rave culture is no longer just for younger people, and women in midlife are soaking in every ounce of fun, freedom, community, and release. “They don't want to be defined by their age, but more importantly, they don't want to be restricted by it,” says O’Grady. “Saying, ‘I want to dress up in my sequins, I want to put my face on, I want to go and have a dance, I want to stay out all night and shrug off my responsibilities for a little while, I want all of that and why shouldn't I?’”

For Manson, getting ready is part of the appeal, and she’s collected a variety of vibrant, fun outfits to go out in. “It's almost like creating a bit of an identity, which I'm quite enjoying,” she says. At this stage of life, raving has given her a way to reinvent herself.

Midlife can chip away at a woman’s confidence and leave her feeling overlooked. Raving pushes back on that by giving women a place to be bold and seen. As Karen D. puts it, “Women of my age can often disappear or become invisible, and it's almost the opposite of that.”

Since her husband’s death, Manson has made a point of pushing herself to try new things. Raving has given her lasting memories, a fresh outlook, and a crew of friends who aren’t ready to stop dancing anytime soon. “I live with the feeling that life’s very short and precious,” she says, “so seize the moment.”

#4997. $14.7B in ‘Lost’ Bitcoin Has Moved Since 2018: Report

$14.7B in ‘Lost’ Bitcoin Has Moved Since 2018: Report

Bitcoin that hasn't been moved in years is sometimes considered "lost" by industry onlookers, and one lawsuit is arguing that they've been "abandoned." But since 2018, roughly 10,000 supposedly lost Bitcoin wallets have sprung back to life.

Pseudonymous developer Quickben22 built a list in 2018 of 92,076 Bitcoin wallets that hadn't moved funds in more than six years, assuming the owners had lost their keys. Eight years later, the developer revisited the list to discover that 9,990 of those wallets have since moved a total of approximately 245,000 BTC, or just over $14.7 billion at Bitcoin's current price.

"Dormant is not the same as lost," Quickben22 told Decrypt. "I expected nearly all of the 92,076 addresses to still be silent after 8 years. About 89% are, but 9,990 have moved, and 14+ year old addresses are still waking up."

That distinction matters, as the findings come as a New York lawsuit brought by a pseudonymous plaintiff known as 'Noah Doe' tries to claim 39,069 dormant Bitcoin addresses as abandoned property, including wallets linked to Bitcoin creator Satoshi Nakamoto.

The plaintiffs argue the coins are "abandoned" under New York's lost property law. They say they found the wallets, reported them to the NYPD, and sent the owners notice by attaching on-chain messages to tiny Bitcoin transactions.

"It's like writing down the addresses of every locked house on a street, telling the police, and claiming whatever is inside because nobody answered the door," Quickben22 said.

Some wallets linked to the suit have since woken up, with several moving funds earlier this year—including one first funded in 2013 that shifted 411.45 BTC in October, then worth $33.4 million. One pseudonymous holder has also filed a motion to dismiss the case, claiming to still control a named wallet.

Quickben22's list was originally built for an app called Bitcoin Key Hunter, which guesses private keys at random and checks them against the dormant addresses in the hope of landing on one.

"It's like playing the lottery, but with much, much smaller odds," he said, before breaking down the math: roughly 1 in 10^43 across the whole list. "Those are about the odds of winning five Powerballs in a row," he added.

Quickben22 did not respond to Decrypt's query on whether he has successfully guessed the keys to any of the listed wallets.

It is impossible to know who exactly moved the funds from the supposedly lost wallets—it might not even be the original owner. An original owner tidying up old funds looks the same on-chain as someone who found a seed phrase in a drawer, or a hacker who got hold of a key that was never theirs.

"The blockchain shows that someone could sign, but not who," Quickben22 wrote.

Even when a wallet really is lost, the owner doesn't always let go.

Welshman James Howells has spent more than a decade trying to recover a hard drive holding around 8,000 BTC, which his then-girlfriend accidentally threw out during an office clear-out in 2013. He traced it to a landfill in Newport, Wales, and spent years seeking permission to dig it up, until a judge dismissed his case on environmental grounds. Howells called the ruling a "stitch-up."

Last year, he offered the local council £2.5 million to buy the landfill outright, Decrypt reported. The council didn't respond. He has since given up the search and is instead launching Ceiniog, a Bitcoin layer-2 network with a token he says is backed by the buried coins he can't access.

“MY view is this: As long as YOU (or anyone else in the world) can view the balance [and can] verify for yourself that it still contains 8,000 Bitcoin, then [the] Ceiniog coin is fully backed with its value,” he told Decrypt last year. “If those coins ever moved, Ceiniog instantly loses its backing and value. I am guaranteeing that those coins will never move—because the private key is on a [hard drive] in a landfill.”

Howells' 8,000 BTC haven't moved since 2013. On paper, they look exactly like the coins on Quickben22's list, and the kind the Noah Doe lawsuit wants declared abandoned.

#4995. Ukraine Legalizes Crypto After One-Day Delay

Home » Regulations » Ukraine Legalizes Crypto After One-Day Delay

Crypto-embracing Bill No. 10225-d gets the highest-priority treatment following a slight procedural delay.

Ukraine’s parliament has approved a bill to bring cryptocurrency trading, custody and taxation under a formal legal framework.

The measure, Bill No. 10225-d, passed after lawmakers postponed consideration a day earlier, a pause that had raised questions about its immediate path despite renewed support from the parliamentary finance committee for the revised text.

The Ukraine crypto bill is designed to legalize and regulate the domestic virtual-asset market rather than leave it in a largely undefined legal space.

Its scope includes tax treatment for crypto activity as well as rules for trading platforms and custodial services.

That approach would place businesses handling customer assets under a clearer licensing and compliance structure.

BREAKING: Ukraine officially passes law to LEGALIZE crypto, effective July 1, 2027. pic.twitter.com/6KxnNa7N2b

The framework comes into practice on July 1, 2027. It offers more certainty over how digital-asset transactions are treated by authorities, though implementation details will matter as much as the legislation itself.

Ukraine has maintained an active crypto sector despite the strains of war, with digital assets playing a visible role in fundraising and cross-border transfers.

Formalizing the market has therefore carried significance beyond ordinary financial regulation: it could help define how crypto businesses operate in an economy still managing exceptional pressures with the fifth year of war with Russia coming along.

The Ukraine crypto bill’s journey shows how quickly crypto policy can shift even when lawmakers broadly support regulation.

BREAKING: Zelensky President of Ukraine officially legalizes Bitcoin & crypto after parliament passes the bill with 271 vote pic.twitter.com/qt9C7jcNVK

The November 24, 2026 postponement followed committee backing for a revised version, while the subsequent passage points to a resolution of at least some of those immediate obstacles.

Questions remain over the final tax mechanics, the timing of licensing requirements and which agencies will oversee different parts of the sector. Market participants will also watch for secondary rules that determine the practical burden on exchanges, brokers and wallet providers.

Ukraine’s crypto move matters because it adds another sizable European market pursuing rules for digital assets rather than relying on prohibition or legal ambiguity.

The Ukraine crypto legislation may give local firms a route toward greater legitimacy, but the ultimate test will be whether the resulting framework is workable enough to retain innovation while improving crypto oversight.

#4994. Vitamin C May Lower Your Risk of Cancer from Certain Processed Foods

Here’s what experts say about the “promising” new study results.

While diving into a plate of bacon or noshing on some salami is always tasty, there’s been growing concern that compounds found in cured meats may raise the risk of cancer. Specifically, once they hit your stomach, nitrates and nitrites found in these foods can spark a chain reaction called nitrosation that allows carcinogens to develop. This isn’t just a meat-eating issue either: fruits and vegetables that have grown in areas affected by pollution can also lead to this chain reaction.

Now, new research published in the Journal of Theoretical Biology suggests a possible solution: Take a carefully timed vitamin C supplement. It can cut this chain reaction and, in theory, lower the odds that carcinogens will develop after eating certain foods linked to this reaction, according to the findings.

Researchers stress that this doesn’t mean you should pop a vitamin C every time you have bacon. But the findings raise a lot of questions about why this may work and how to actually put it into practice in a safe way. Here’s what the researcher behind the study and dietitians want you to keep in mind.

Meet the experts: Gordon R. McNicol, PhD, lead study author and postdoctoral scholar in the Department of Applied Mathematics at the University of Waterloo; Jessica Cording, MS, RD, registered dietitian and author of The Little Book of Game-Changers; and Keri Gans, MS, RD, registered dietitian and author of The Small Change Diet.

For the study, researchers developed a mathematical model that simulates how nitrates and nitrites travel through the body, and where they undergo chemical changes. The model looked at a range of areas, including the salivary glands, stomach, small intestine, and plasma (i.e. the liquid part of your blood). Researchers discovered that having vitamin C alongside foods that contain nitrates and nitrites may halt chain reactions that happen in the body, including nitrosation, which makes substances that are linked to cancer development.

The researchers also looked at whether taking vitamin C after each meal could help, and found that it may reduce the formation of nitrosation products linked with cancer risk. The boost was most meaningful when people had foods that contained nitrates and nitrites, like salami, bacon, and other processed meats.

The researchers also theorized that this may explain why certain types of produce that happen to contain both vitamin C and nitrates (like spinach) don’t seem to increase cancer risk, while others do.

It’s important to stress this: The study was based on a mathematical model and was not a clinical trial or data analysis. Because of that, it's hard to draw too many conclusions right now.

Still, this link isn’t out of nowhere. “Under acidic conditions in the stomach, nitrites can undergo chemical reactions that lead to the formation of potentially harmful N-nitroso compounds,” says Gordon R. McNicol, PhD, lead study author and postdoctoral scholar in the Department of Applied Mathematics at the University of Waterloo. “Vitamin C can interfere with these reactions, reducing the formation of these compounds.”

Why vitamin C? “Vitamin C is an antioxidant,” points out Jessica Cording, MS, RD, registered dietitian and author of The Little Book of Game-Changers. Meaning, it helps to neutralize unstable molecules in the body—and may do the same for nitrosation.

But the effectiveness of vitamin C depends on when it’s in the stomach compared to when these reactions happen, McNicol adds. “Our simulations suggest that taking vitamin C shortly after meals could be particularly effective, as this allows vitamin C to overlap more closely with periods when nitrosation would otherwise be relatively high,” he says.

Experts stress that it’s important to keep the study in perspective. “While the findings are promising, more research is needed to determine whether taking vitamin C after meals actually reduces cancer risk,” says Keri Gans, MS, RD, registered dietitian and author of The Small Change Diet.

Cording agrees, stressing that while the findings are “promising,” they’re still just based on a mathematical model at this point. “That said, getting enough vitamin C and other antioxidants, alongside nutrients like fiber and other beneficial plant compounds, has been associated with reduced risk of disease and with overall immune system function,” Cording says. “There are lots of great reasons to include vitamin-C rich fruits and vegetables throughout the day.”

There are other things to consider, like practicality and safety. “Our research does not establish that taking vitamin C supplements after every meal is necessary or advisable,” McNicol says. “Although our simulations suggest that dividing a fixed daily supplement across meals may be more effective than taking the same amount at once, further experimental and clinical studies are needed to determine whether these strategies are effective and safe in people.”

High doses of vitamin C from supplements can also lead to GI discomfort, including nausea and diarrhea, Gans points out.

For now, this is more of an interesting finding vs. an actual dietary recommendation. “Until we have more research, there's no reason to recommend intentionally adding extra vitamin C, whether from food or supplements, after every meal specifically to reduce cancer risk,” Gans says.

Carina Hsieh, MPH, is the deputy features editor of Women’s Health. She has more than a decade’s worth of experience working in media and has covered everything from beauty, fashion, travel, lifestyle, pets, to health.

She began her career as an intern in the fashion closet at Cosmopolitan where she worked her way up to Senior Sex & Relationships Editor. While covering women’s health there, she discovered her passion for health service journalism and took a break to get her Masters in Public Health. Post-grad school, she worked as a freelance writer and as The Daily Beast’s first Beauty, Health, and Wellness Reporter.

Carina is an alum of the Fashion Institute of Technology and the Yale School of Public Health. She and her French Bulldog, Bao Bao, split their time between Brooklyn and Connecticut. She enjoys reformer Pilates, (slow) running, and smelling the fancy toiletries in boutique fitness class locker rooms.

#4992. GTA 6 PC Ports ‘Nuked’ Just Days Before Devs Expected It to Be Playable

GTA 6 PC Ports ‘Nuked’ Just Days Before Devs Expected It to Be Playable

Several major projects attempting to port Grand Theft Auto 6 to PC have been "nuked," according to community insiders. It comes as developers thought a playable port was just days away, after notorious Rockstar hacker Cyberleek released the game's files.

Both the Leonida GitHub page and the GTA6Modding Discord server—two of the most serious attempts at porting the latest Grand Theft Auto title to PC—have been removed. Other servers also involved in the AI-powered porting scene, such as the Chasm Server, have also locked down.

"Leonida and GTA6Modding have both been nuked," Freakman, a Chasm Server mod, wrote on Discord. "We have no affiliation with Cyberleek," they added. "Multiple servers have been struck, we're staying low for tonight."

Cyberleek released an Xbox build of GTA 6 on November 19, the day the game launched on consoles. However, they held back the main executable needed to run it and promised they'd release it if the CYBERLEEK meme coin hit a $15 million market cap.

Porting projects had been preparing for that file, expecting it'd be the key to making the port playable. The scene leans heavily on AI coding tools to speed up the reverse engineering needed to get console games running on PC, with developers describing themselves as "vibe coders."

The meme coin missed its $15 million target, but Cyberleek released the executable on Monday anyway. The next day, several GTA 6 porting projects were shut down.

"They're taking out servers left and right that are mentioning the leak," Chasm community member Weedgoose told Decrypt. "Some servers take the hit while others are going dark and are waiting for the flames to extinguish."

Some of the impacted community members have moved to alternative messaging platforms that are more private than Discord, Weedgoose said.

It appears the Leonida GitHub was removed by its creator, an apparent high school student, as it shows a 404 error page rather than a DMCA takedown page. That said, there's no way of knowing if the creator received a cease and desist (or similar correspondence) that led to this decision.

Chasm mod Freakman did not respond to Decrypt's request for comment regarding why the server has gone dark.

Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar's parent company, has been going after the leaks for months. In August, it filed subpoenas asking Discord and Microsoft, which owns GitHub, to hand over data that could help identify Cyberleek.

Rockstar has yet to announce an official PC version of GTA 6 yet. GamesBeat reported in October that one could arrive in Q1 of 2027—and the prospect of an unofficial port releasing in advance of that would likely dent sales.

Rockstar did not respond to Decrypt's request for comment.
