#4990. Jade Cargill Was a Basketball Player Before the WWE. Here’s What Changed Everything

The 34-year-old wrestling superstar stops byThe Huddle ahead of her appearance on Survivor Series: WarGames on November 28th.

Given the ease with which WWE superstar Jade Cargill delivers a pump kick or spinebuster, it’s hard to believe the 34-year-old hasn’t spent her entire life in the ring. But growing up, Jade was obsessed with a different sport: basketball. In college, she was a forward/guard for the Jacksonville University team then went on to play overseas in France.

The experience of being a team player has come in handy for Jade as she navigates the world of wrestling. Sure, it may often look like a one-on-one competition, but Jade says that, if anything, it’s more like a dance.

“I can only be as great as my partner,” she tells editors Abigail Cuffey, Amanda Lucci, and Jacqueline Andriakos on the latest episode of The Huddle. “I can't do this by myself.”

Despite having been a part of the WWE since 2023, Jade admits she’s still a “rookie” compared to her ‘dance’ partners—the other women in the league, who inspire her every day. “I've been placed in a very amazing environment with women who strive for greatness, and that's what I want to do,” she says.

As she prepares to lead a five-woman team at Survivor Series: WarGames on November 28, Jade talks about her unconventional path to wrestling, making peace with mistakes, and the advice she wants every kid watching her to hear.

Jade’s journey to becoming a professional wrestler is the stuff of motivational sports movies. A stay-at-home mom (she took time off work as a child psychologist to raise her daughter), Jade was simply training in the gym to get strong after pregnancy when she was introduced to WWE veteran Mark Henry, who asked if she’d ever considered a career in wrestling.

“I was like, ‘Why not?’” she recalls thinking. “I had a kid and put my life on hold for a little bit. I wanted to do something more. I was like, ‘This body is not done.’ [I] went to a tryout, had no experience at all.”

Jade left that tryout bruised and battered—and determined to improve. And so she trained and trained and trained some more. She couldn’t get enough. “I just loved it,” she says. “It's athletics, yes, but also it's improvising, but also it's acting, but also it's your natural instinct. It’s all these things wrapped into one that I just didn't want to put down.”

All that work eventually paid off: Jade made her professional wrestling debut with All Elite Wrestling in 2020 and then joined the WWE three years later.

Despite all the training and preparation that goes into a match, Jade admits that not a single one has been “perfect.” But in the case where she stumbles off the ropes or throws a lousy punch, Jade simply follows the old maxim, the show must go on.

“I just kind of have the mindset that these things happen,” she says. “If you do have a mishap, you can't sell it—[the audience doesn’t] know what's going on. You just got to keep going with the punches.”

Jade also gives a lot of credit to her fellow competitors, who often pick her up—if not physically, then emotionally—after a match, letting her know she’s not alone.

“I remember my coworker Naomi sent me a clip of her falling, and she was like, ‘Just to show you...’ And I was like, ‘Okay, all right. It happens,’” Jade says. “You’ve just got to keep on going and make your next match the best match.”

As a mom, Jade knows how powerful an adult’s example can be—whether it’s a parent’s or a performer’s. Ultimately, she hopes kids are inspired by her hard work and determination, both in and out of the ring, and if they can take away any message, it would be this: “Don't let anyone tell you who you are,” she says. “Don't let society put you in a box. Go out there and take on the world.”

And when a new opportunity presents itself, don’t be afraid to give it a try. “If you would have told me five years ago, I would be wrestling. I would have laughed,” she says. “And look at me now.”

To hear more from Jade—including her no-frills recovery program—click play on the latest episode of The Huddle above.

#4988. Morning Minute: Jensen Returns, Markets Soar (Except Crypto)

Morning Minute: Jensen Returns, Markets Soar (Except Crypto)

Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner. The analysis and opinions expressed are his own and do not necessarily reflect those of Decrypt. And check out our daily news show 'FOMO HOUR' covering all of the top stories and market action.

Six days after Nvidia’s board chair told investors “the Nvidia board does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” the board voted unanimously to reinstate him as president, CEO and director, effective immediately.

Nvidia shares rose 33% to around $167, adding roughly a trillion dollars of market value in a session. Huang’s personal net worth climbed about $36.6 billion on his 3.5% stake, moving him to 13th on the Forbes global list. Short sellers took roughly $12.2 billion in paper losses, their worst single day since at least 2019, which wiped out the $10.5 billion they had booked the prior week.

The stock market absolutely ripped on the news. The Nasdaq closed up 6.51% at 24,089, its best day since April 2025. The S&P gained 4.7%, the Dow was +3%, and the VIX collapsed 25.8% to 26.62.

Bitcoin went along with the ride—for a few hours. It touched $63,929 intraday, up 5.1%, then spent the afternoon handing it back and finished near $61,000, barely up on the day. The ETFs used the pump to exit more, with BTC ETFs seeing another $570M in outflows on the day.

ETH and other majors also closed red. Alts gave back their gains. And the CMC top 20 index managed just 0.20% gain.

That’s a 19 to 1 ratio between what the Nasdaq captured and what Bitcoin kept, on the same catalyst, on the same day. Pain for the crypto bulls.

What makes it even more painful, is that crypto fell with AI stocks the whole way down, and the standard explanation was that both trade on the same liquidity and the same risk appetite. Monday tested that and the correlation fell through. The AI trade got a catalyst and markets bounced. Crypto didn’t bounce with it.

As for Nvidia’s reversal decision itself, questions remain to say the least. The board says it was satisfied with Huang’s “candor and ability to lead,” and that input from senior U.S. officials left it confident his return “poses no national security risk.” Trump publicly pushed for it and said the board had sought assurance on the espionage allegations. What actually changed between November 17 and November 23 hasn’t been explained. The independent directors’ investigation is still open, and Nvidia is now standing up a board committee for national security and export-control oversight plus recruiting a chief compliance officer.

Perhaps answers will trickle out over time. The AI trade may not need them anyway. And crypto, well, it's in its own world right now, waiting for its own catalysts (likely quantum-related). But it’s very unclear that catalyst is coming in 2026, and it’s becoming clear that many are not interested in waiting for the answers…

#4986. Why So Many New Moms Are Told to Wait to Exercise Again—and What the Research Really Says

The six-week postpartum checkup was never meant to be about fitness.

Earlier this year, trainer and WH advisory board member Sohee Carpenter, CSCS, posted an Instagram Reel challenging some conventional postpartum advice: Don’t work out until your ob-gyn clears you at your six-week follow-up appointment. Her point wasn’t that new moms should rush back to the gym. It was that one timeline can’t fit everyone. Some women are ready to move sooner, and others need more time.

“I feel like so many people get angry because they assume we mean you're going to be doing a one-rep max back squat a week after you have a baby,” Carpenter says. “But that's definitely not what we're saying.” (By “we,” she means trainers who keep up with the latest research on pregnancy and postpartum exercise.)

The problem, Carpenter explains, is that the six-week rule isn’t based on evidence. On the contrary, research suggests that this type of blanket advice doesn’t make sense for something as personal as postpartum recovery. When you return to exercise after childbirth should depend on your own symptoms, not a date on the calendar.

“There's really nothing magical about the six-week time point,” says Margie Davenport, PhD, a professor of kinesiology at the University of Alberta and chair of the 2025 Canadian Guidelines for Physical Activity for Pregnancy and Postpartum—the first-ever exercise guidelines to specifically focus on evidence-based suggestions for that first year postpartum. In the U.S., the main guidance from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) covers pregnancy and the postpartum period together. ACOG’s guidance points in the same direction, though: It says many women can start exercising again within days of an uncomplicated birth. In fact, “there is no identified ideal time to return,” Davenport says.

Based on the wide range of comments on Carpenter’s post—some supportive, some hypercritical, and still others asking more questions to try to better understand this shift away from the advice they’ve always heard—there’s still a lot of confusion around postpartum exercise. So we asked experts to break down what the research actually says, and how to approach working out in this new chapter of life.

In many cultures, the first 30 or 40 days postpartum is traditionally considered a protected time to rest, relax, and recover, Davenport says. In Chinese culture, it’s called zuo yuezi, which translates to “sitting the month.” In many Latin American and Latino communities, it’s known as “la cuarentena,” a nod to its roughly 40-day length. In South Korea, it’s sanhujori, or “postpartum care.”

These traditions carry deep cultural significance and are meant to offer real healing and support after birth from one’s community (they put “it takes a village” into practice). They’re rooted in caregiving and cultural custom, and they were never meant to serve as a medical timeline for when it’s safe to start exercising.

In Western medicine, six weeks has become an important medical benchmark in postpartum recovery—and, over time, a default point for returning to exercise too. “At that point, your uterus should be back to its pre-pregnancy state, and so a lot of the gynecologic changes should be fairly reversed by that point,” says Rita Deering, DPT, PhD, associate professor of exercise science and director of the Pelvic Health, Exercise & Musculoskeletal (PHEM) Research Laboratory at Marquette University.

The first six weeks after birth are also when the risk of complications like high blood pressure and infection is highest, Deering says, which is part of why that window became an important medical checkpoint (even though some pregnancy-related changes take longer to resolve). But, she says, “it was never intended to be about exercise.”

So how did six weeks become the exercise rule? Before researchers knew much about how safe it is to exercise during pregnancy and after birth, working out was considered potentially risky, Deering says. There wasn’t strong evidence that exercise wouldn’t slow healing or raise the odds of complications. So the most cautious advice was simply to wait until a doctor confirmed you’d healed enough to resume physical activity.

To come up with the 2025 Canadian Guidelines, researchers did a deep dive of all the available research on the topic, which included 574 unique studies organized into seven systematic reviews based on 21 different outcomes of postpartum exercise—such as depression and anxiety, low-back pain, injuries, glucose and blood pressure levels, and more. They also assembled an international panel of experts to give their recommendations.

Their advice: Start light-intensity physical activity and mobilization (think: carrying your baby around your home, a slow walk down the block, pelvic floor physical therapy) right away. From there, progress as you feel ready to moderate-to-vigorous activity such as brisk walking, resistance training, and running at your own pace—as long as tears and incisions have sufficiently healed and you don’t experience additional bleeding with exercise. (As mentioned, ACOG similarly recommends that women can return to postnatal exercise within days after an uncomplicated birth.)

Based on the research, there are no “absolute contraindications” to exercise postpartum, Davenport says—meaning no condition would rule out exercise entirely. There are some relative contraindications, she explains, “where you might have to delay a little bit or modify the type of activity that you're doing.” Examples include severe abdominal pain, extreme fatigue, and C-section incision pain that worsens with activity. All warrant a conversation with your doctor before starting.

Want to Know More About Lifting While Pregnant? Start Here

Pelvic floor symptoms, like leaking urine or a feeling of heaviness in the vagina, aren’t a reason to stop exercising altogether. If you notice signs of pelvic floor dysfunction, the guidelines recommend starting slowly and building up gradually instead. “Some leakage is okay,” Davenport says. “It means that the training that you’re doing is just overloading the muscle.”

Many people, including plenty of commenters on Carpenter’s Reel, worry that exercising after birth will damage the pelvic floor and cause dysfunction. But the evidence doesn’t support that. In fact, those muscles will likely be better off if you resume training, especially if you do exercises to target them in particular. “Engaging in pelvic floor muscle training reduces your risk of urinary incontinence by around 37 percent,” Davenport says. Additionally, if you stop all exercise because you're leaking a little bit, “this can actually mean that you're missing out on those other benefits.”

One caveat: If you’re leaking a lot, or it’s getting worse over time, “you probably need to pull it back,” Davenport says. That means being more selective about the moves you choose. For example, you might skip long runs and high-impact moves like jump squats for now, adds Sheridan Skye, a registered nurse, pre- and postnatal fitness coach, and founder of The Female Fitness Formula. Stick with lower-impact exercises, then build up gradually as you get stronger and your symptoms level off or improve.

At the end of the day, every body, birth, and recovery is vastly different. “Some people have a very uncomplicated labor and delivery and pregnancy; for others, it's quite complex,” says Davenport. “It only makes sense that the way that they're returning and what time they're actually returning is also going to be quite individualized.”

For some new moms, six weeks is too soon, and a blanket deadline only adds stress. “Maybe they aren't sleeping or they don't have the support to be able to return [to exercise] at six weeks,” Davenport says. On the flip side, for someone who had a straightforward delivery and is itching to get moving again, “telling them to wait for six weeks with no evidence to support it is also inappropriate.”

In fact, exercise can offer significant benefits during postpartum recovery, even before the six-week mark. “It improves muscle and bone density that we lose throughout pregnancy,” Skye says. Postpartum exercise is associated with a 45 percent reduction in the odds of developing postpartum depression, and starting before 12 weeks is even more beneficial.

It’s also associated with a 28 percent reduction in the risk of developing diabetes postpartum. Exercise even improves sleep quality, Skye notes. “Women tend to feel more energized and like they've experienced more rest, even if they haven't,” she says. (Anyone who’s survived a 3 a.m. feeding stretch knows that’s no small thing!)

There is also evidence that exercise in general can help to decrease pain, says Deering, and research links sedentary behavior to lumbopelvic (the areas of the lower back and pelvis) pain. “So if you are having pain, movement might be what you need to help with that.”

For many people, it may be difficult to know if you’re truly ready. “Especially when you're postpartum, it can feel like you are super out of touch with your body sensations, especially if you're not sleeping well,” Carpenter says.

If you're at the point where you're thinking about it, but are nervous or unsure or just overwhelmed by having another decision to make, Davenport recommends taking the Get Active Questionnaire for Postpartum—a tool that her team designed as part of the 2025 guideline. It can help you quickly understand if you’re ready to start from a medical perspective. That can help give you some reassurance.

There can also be “a lot of fear involved,” Carpenter says, especially if you had a C-section or are healing from a vaginal tear. In that case, “you’re probably going to be a bit hesitant,” which is completely understandable. Starting slower and lighter than you think you need to is perfectly fine as you get reacquainted with your body. “The first several sessions are really about mentally trying to get that confidence back,” she says.

As you go, pay attention to how your body responds. Leaking, for instance? That’s not a reason to stop exercising, but you may want to adjust your workout to reduce it. More bleeding, new pain, or a sense that something just doesn’t feel right are signs to stop, reassess, and possibly scale back. If they don’t improve, check in with your doctor. “It’s really about setting your ego aside and being willing to modify, even if it’s one rep to the next, based on how you’re feeling right at that time,” Carpenter says.

And if you feel physically ready but aren’t quite there mentally? “It’s okay to honor those feelings,” Deering says, “and to recognize that it’s okay to give yourself some time.” Whether that’s two weeks, six weeks, or six months, the right moment to start moving is the one that works for you.

#4985. CertiK Trains Interpol Investigators to Trace and Freeze Stolen Crypto

CertiK Trains Interpol Investigators to Trace and Freeze Stolen Crypto

Blockchain security firm CertiK trained police investigators from across Asia and the South Pacific in tracing stolen crypto and securing asset freezes at an INTERPOL meeting in Hanoi, the company said.

The 3rd INTERPOL Asia and South Pacific Working Group Meeting on Cybercrime ran from October 27 to October 30, 2026. It was organized by INTERPOL's Cybercrime Directorate and Vietnam's Ministry of Public Security. CertiK said senior law enforcement officials from 20 countries attended, with stablecoin issuer Tether and South Korean exchange Upbit among the other private-sector partners.

CertiK's sessions focused on the two stages of recovering stolen crypto: mapping how funds move after a theft, then using that evidence to ask exchanges to freeze them.

Officers worked through a real wallet-compromise case, using open-source block explorers and CertiK's compliance software to follow stolen funds through token swaps, cross-chain bridges and intermediary wallets to three deposit addresses at an exchange. The exercise included spotting address-poisoning decoys, which attackers use to send investigators down false trails.

CertiK's team then explained the process for contacting the exchange, using its law enforcement portal and filing formal requests to freeze the funds.

Other sessions covered how to read wallet activity before and after a suspicious transaction, how smart contract vulnerabilities and audit findings can inform an investigation, and how to tell apart attacks involving compromised signing keys, phishing and social engineering.

"Investigators need both a clear picture of how an attack happened and a practical route to act on the evidence," Esme Pau, CertiK's head of capital markets and policy, said in a statement.

Fellow security firm Group-IB, which also presented, tweeted that the four-day meeting drew more than 80 participants from over 43 countries and regions. INTERPOL's working group for heads of regional cybercrime units first met in Manila in September 2024.

The training comes as INTERPOL steps up its work on crypto-enabled crime. In July 2026, it said that a 20-year-old Thai suspect's wallet had moved more than $122.5 million in romance-scam proceeds in 10 months, using cross-chain swaps to hide the trail. The case was one of many in Operation First Light, a 97-country sweep that led to 5,811 arrests.

💫 Group-IB participated in the 3rd @INTERPOL_Cyber Asia & South Pacific Cybercrime Working Group Meeting in Hanoi, Vietnam, held from 27–30 October 2026. Led by INTERPOL’s Cybercrime Directorate - Asia & South Pacific Cybercrime Operations Desk and co-hosted by Vietnam’s… pic.twitter.com/tYaKEUnaXL

— Group-IB Global (@GroupIB) November 3, 2026

In October 2026, Operation Serengeti III recovered more than $105 million across 21 African countries and shut two illegal crypto mining centers in Angola. It followed Operation Catalyst, in which INTERPOL and Afripol arrested 83 people in 2025. INTERPOL's member countries also designated scam-compound networks, which channel billions of dollars through crypto, a transnational criminal threat in November 2025.

Tether, which can freeze USDT at flagged addresses, has become a regular partner in such investigations. In April 2026, it froze more than $344 million in USDT across two Tron addresses in coordination with U.S. authorities. That figure predates the largest theft of the year. The FBI has attributed October's $6.4 billion hack of Binance, which took place during the Hanoi meeting, to North Korea's TraderTraitor group. North Korea has denied involvement.

#4981. Justice Department Moves to Forfeit $1.1B in USDC From North Korea's Binance Hack

Justice Department Moves to Forfeit $1.1B in USDC From North Korea's Binance Hack

The U.S. Justice Department has moved to permanently take control of more than $1.1 billion in crypto stolen by North Korean hackers in the record $6.4 billion theft from Binance.

The department filed a civil forfeiture claim on Monday for the funds, which are held in USDC, the stablecoin issued by Circle, it said. The assets were already subject to a restraining order the government had requested after the hack, and Circle provided "valuable assistance," the department said.

The filing is part of a wider U.S. effort to help Binance recover the stolen funds. Since the October 29 hack, the U.S. has helped freeze, seize or return more than $2.9 billion in crypto, according to the department. That is up from the $2.7 billion in frozen assets it reported on November 12, when it said it had court approval to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion.

"Swift coordination between the government and private sector partners helped prevent a substantial portion of those assets from disappearing," Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the department's Criminal Division said in a statement.

Secret Service investigators identified and froze stolen funds "within minutes of the hack," said Todd Bratz, special agent in charge of the agency's Criminal Investigations Division. The Secret Service is investigating the case alongside the FBI and IRS Criminal Investigation.

The FBI has attributed the theft to TraderTraitor, which the Justice Department describes as members of the North Korean military. North Korea has denied involvement, and Binance has set aside $6.34 billion to cover customer losses.

Stablecoin issuers Tether and Circle froze funds after the hack. But the hackers have kept moving what they still control. After two weeks of inactivity, wallets tied to the hack began moving Ethereum in mid-November.

At least $247 million has since been funneled through Bitcoin coinjoins, a mixing technique that pools funds to obscure their origin, blockchain analytics firm Elliptic said on Monday. Elliptic estimates that about $2.85 billion has been frozen and that roughly $2.35 billion remains in addresses tied to the theft.

Binance has also pursued the funds through the courts, winning a $6.5 billion freezing order from Abu Dhabi courts that can be served on wallet holders via the blockchain.

#4978. Europol Traces $28M in Crypto Behind Europe's Illegal Streaming Industry

Europol Traces $28M in Crypto Behind Europe's Illegal Streaming Industry

Law enforcement agencies from 11 countries have traced more than €26 million ($28 million) in crypto payments linked to illegal TV streaming services, in an operation that brought in crypto exchanges Binance and Coinbase and blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis, Europol said on Tuesday.

The five-day operation, held at the Spanish National Police headquarters in Seville from November 16 to November 20, 2026, disrupted 57 illegal IPTV services. Investigators also identified 321 websites illegally offering copyrighted content, which together receive more than 7.3 million visits a year. Analysis of the crypto transactions is continuing.

Investigators are increasingly targeting the money behind illegal streaming services, not just the services themselves.

Last week, Chainalysis joined Europol, law enforcement from 11 countries, and industry partners including Binance and Coinbase in Seville for a five-day… pic.twitter.com/XqV0Hima26

— Chainalysis (@chainalysis) November 24, 2026

IPTV, or internet protocol television, services sell access to television channels, live sports and films over the internet. Illegal providers charge a few euros a month for unauthorized access to premium content, often taking subscription payments in crypto, according to Europol.

During the operation, investigators traced suspicious transactions across blockchains to find links between illegal services, the crypto wallets receiving payments and the people controlling them.

Europol said the operation reflected a shift in strategy. Rather than focusing only on shutting down streaming services, investigators are increasingly targeting the financial infrastructure behind them, because taking a service offline does not necessarily stop the people running it.

Europol has gone after criminals' crypto in other cases, too. In June 2026, its Operation Endgame froze more than €41 million ($47 million) in crypto linked to infostealer malware, and in March it helped disrupt a proxy network whose payment platform had received more than $5.7 million in crypto.

Around 40 people took part, including 30 law enforcement officers from Belgium, Bulgaria, Croatia, Greece, Ireland, Italy, the Netherlands, Portugal, Romania, Spain and the U.S.

Europol coordinated the operation through its Intellectual Property Crime Coordinated Coalition, a unit supported by the European Union Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO), which also took part alongside INTERPOL and the Audio-visual Anti-Piracy Alliance (AAPA). The information gathered will feed into national investigations to identify suspects and trace assets.

An estimated 60 million people in Europe use unauthorized IPTV services, costing legitimate providers €4.83 billion ($5.3 billion) a year and governments a further €1.08 billion ($1.2 billion) in lost taxes, according to AAPA figures cited by Europol. Demand appears to be growing: visits to websites offering sign-ups for illegal IPTV services rose 10% in 2023, an EUIPO study found.

Europol ran a similar operation last year. In November 2025, a week-long cyber-patrol in Alicante, Spain, traced about $55 million in crypto linked to piracy services and referred 25 illegal IPTV services to crypto providers for disruption, The Record reported at the time.

Crypto also features in older piracy cases. In Germany, the alleged operator of defunct piracy site Movie2K has been offered a deal to end his money laundering and tax evasion trial if he hands over 40,000 BTC. Prosecutors believe he still holds about 56,000 BTC, bought with proceeds from the site before it shut down in 2013.

The offer came days after German lawmakers approved new powers allowing customs officials to seize crypto and other assets of unclear origin without first opening a criminal case.

The wide headband is plush and fits securely onto the head without being too tight. MH senior gear and commerce editor Ryan Brower throws it in his gym bag whenever he has strength training on deck. He also appreciates the adjustable smooth slider for a custom fit, calling it a fluid mechanism.

The headphones use 12 microphones to isolate and cancel out sound to deliver an immersive listening experience. Vocals and instruments sound balanced and rich, with Brower calling the sound quality superb. Battery life can run for up to 30 hours, while just three minutes of charging can provide three hours—perfect if you’re in a rush to hit the gym.

Brower’s only gripes are the lack of sweat resistance for high-intensity activities, like running or spinning, and that it feels a little bulky. So, he reserves it for less strenuous pursuits.

If you’re into an over-ear design in headphones, you know they can get hot and sweaty fast. But the Skullcandy Crusher 540 headphones feel surprisingly breathable on—for an over-ear headphone. The ear cups are made from a lightweight material that feels breezy against your ears, minimizing extra sweating while you work out.

These headphones also have an impressive battery life of 40 hours, which is only second on our list to the Powerbeats Pro 2. Skullcandy clearly designed these headphones for convenience, with plenty of buttons within easy reach. As a result, you can quickly turn the volume up or down without missing a beat. If active noise cancellation is a must for you, scroll up—while the sound quality on these headphones is excellent, they won’t help you fully tune out the world.

The Skullcandy Crusher 540 headphones don’t have an official IPX rating, but they have a special sweat- and water-resistant nano-coating to protect your gear. (The ear cup pads are also removable for easy cleaning.) A big draw of these headphones is the strong bass, which comes in handy during tough workouts. As someone who loses nearly everything, I appreciate the built-in Tile technology to help you find your headphones with the Tile app if you misplace them.

I first tested the Bose Open Ultra Earbuds last fall, and they’ve been my favorite pair for distance running ever since. These earbuds aren’t going anywhere thanks to a design that’s similar to a clip-on earring. Just gently hook these on your ears and move on. The style is perfect for people like me who have been burned in the past by an earbud falling out and vanishing forever.

As an early morning runner who regularly crosses streets, I appreciate the open-ear audio these earbuds deliver. I can hear my music perfectly, but still can detect things like chirping birds to give me a solid awareness of my surroundings. You can adjust the volume, skip songs, and flip between immersive and stereo sound with a tap on your earbuds, making it easy to switch things up mid-run.

A heads up: If you’ve never used an earbud style like this in the past, you may need to give your ears a little time to build up to wearing them. My ears were a little sore when I first started wearing the Open Ultra Earbuds, but I don’t even feel them when they’re on now. These earbuds are also IPX4 rated for water resistance, so they do just fine with light splashes or rain—just make sure you don't wear these to swim laps.

The earbuds have a seven-hour battery life, which is lower than several others on this list. But I’ve never had an issue with them dying on me. I just pop them in their charging case when they’re not in use.

Some people are going to struggle to get earbuds to fit, no matter what they do. If you have smaller ears and you’re over flipping through different ear tips in hopes something will fit, the Beats Powerbeats Fit are a solid choice. These earbuds actually fit inside your ears like a hearing aid with the help of flexible wingtips that really lock them in there.

These earbuds are small, but they deliver the top-tier sound quality you’ve come to expect from Beats. That includes the options to flip between active noise cancellation and transparency modes, so you can use these to tune out loud gym-goers or to be aware of your surroundings during outdoor workouts.

These earbuds pair seamlessly with Apple and Android phones, making them an equal opportunity headphone. They also have an IPX4 rating for sweat and splash resistance, so you can wear them in the rain, but not to swim laps. While the Powerbeats Fit comes with four different tips, your ears will still need a little time to get used to these before wearing them on, say, a 10-miler.

The earbuds do kind of jam in there, and it can take some time to get used to the feel of the wingtips. But if you’re looking for a discreet pair of headphones that aren’t going anywhere, you can stop your search here.

If you want secure earbuds that aren’t an investment, the Anker Soundcore Sport X20 fits the bill. It costs a third of the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 and shares the same ear-hook design that doesn’t budge when pushing your limits during high-impact workouts. The sound is shockingly premium given the $80 price tag. If I were doing a blind test, I’d think it costs at least $200.

The strong noise cancellation blocks out every peep imaginable at the gym. From loud gym music to weights slamming, I can’t hear a thing except my jams. But when I don’t want to be super locked in, I switch to “normal” mode so I can listen to background noise. This mode is handy when running or walking at night. And when things get too wet during intense grinding sessions, the IP67 sweat-resistance saves me. Although I haven’t tested it while swimming, it can withstand water submersion beyond one meter for about 30 minutes.

The silicone ear hooks are soft, flexible, and extremely comfortable. I find myself reaching for it outside of the gym and often forget it’s even on my ears, which I’m not mad about—it makes a great cool-girl accessory. The only downside of wearing it for too long is that the battery will drain after about eight hours. Luckily, the charging case has two days' worth of battery life—so no excuses to skip a workout.

The Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 are my go-to for long-distance running because of the wrap-around and open-ear design that stays in place. It’s no surprise it’s a TikTok-viral favorite among runners and our editors.

The sweat-resistance rating is one notch below our best overall, with an IP55 score, meaning it can withstand intense rain during rough outdoor conditions. Moisture from sweat is never an issue since the design hangs over the ear and doesn’t go in the canal. It even alerts me with a vibrating beep if moisture is present in the port while charging.

If blocking out noise is your priority, you should consider other options, as this pair doesn’t offer noise cancellation. I don’t love that I can’t be fully engaged in my music, but that’s the trade-off for running safely. Unlike other headphones I tested in this guide, the sound emits outside of the eardrum using bone conduction technology, which is when noise is transmitted through vibrations in the skull to reach the ear. I hear every sound, from people talking to traffic, so I give it a perfect score for maintaining awareness. I deem it an essential pair if you train early in the mornings or at night. Just note it’s not going to be the same listening experience as the Apple AirPods Pro 3, for example.

The battery life is nowhere near the capacity of the Apple AirPods Pro 3, with only about 12 hours of playtime, so I find I have to charge it weekly for an hour. The flip side is that it only takes 10 minutes to get two hours of battery life if I quickly need it before a run.

Full disclosure: They come in two sizes, but tend to run large, which is why I went with the mini size. I ordered the standard size first and had to return them (small head probs).

If you plan on running, spinning, or doing other high-intensity training, it’s best to have headphones that can withstand sweat. They should have an IP rating, which is a protection score for how well electronics can resist water. “IPX4 or higher is perfect for working out,” says Joe Smith, an audio specialist at Music Critic. All options on this list have at least an IPX4 rating.

But our best budget option, the Anker Soundcore Sport X20, has an even better score of IP67, meaning it can handle being submerged in just over one meter of water for 30 minutes. If headphones aren’t made to withstand sweat, it’s best to reserve those for lower-intensity workouts.

Having your headphones die during a half-marathon is not the vibe (been there). Using a pair with good battery life is crucial to ensuring the tunes are always going strong during a long workout. With select pairs, it can be dependent on whether or not select features are in use.

For example, the total playtime for the new Apple AirPods Pro 3 from a single charge (with case) is up to 10 hours with active noise cancellation turned off, but only up to eight hours with it turned on. Carl Prouty, a tech expert at Abt, recommends snagging a model that charges fast in case you forget to plug them in the night before.

Noise cancellation is a function that utilizes a microphone hidden inside the earbud or earcup to analyze frequencies that emit opposite sound waves, thus helping to reduce background noise. Blocking out surrounding noise is great for staying focused and immersed, but it’s not the safest feature in desolate areas like quiet trails, busy streets, or at night.

I prefer an open-ear style to maintain awareness during outdoor runs. If you’re not a fan of that design, other options on this list allow you to turn noise cancellation on and off. “If you still want to be able to hear what's going on around you while also listening to music, look for a model with a good ambient and pass-through mode,” says Prouty.

You have a lot to choose from in a workout headphone, and each has its pros and cons. Earbuds rest inside your ears to deliver sound without bulk. These tend to fit comfortably, but may pop out if you don’t get the fit right. Ear hook earbuds add an extra layer—a hook that goes over your ears—to help combat this issue. There are also open-style headphones that hook over your ears and around the back of your head to keep them in place.

A newer category of these is open earbuds that clip over your ear like a clip-on earring, while nestling into your ear like an earbud. Finally, over-ear headphones have soft cups that fit over your ear for a classic look. While these usually do a good job staying in place, they may feel hotter during intense workouts than other designs.

As a distance runner, I rely on good music to keep me hyped up and entertained on long runs. I’ve tested dozens of pairs of wireless headphones for working out over the past decade and learned what features make pairs stand out. Only workout headphones with good sweat resistance, battery life, noise cancellation, and sound transparency made the final cut.

Because everyone has different needs in a workout headphone, I also leaned on experiences from Women’s Health editors, along with Men’s Health senior gear and reviews editor Ryan Brower. Each pair was used in different environments during cardio and strength training sessions to see how they performed when put to the test during workouts. Those included 5- to 10-mile runs, indoor cycling workouts, HIIT sessions, and more general lifting at the gym.

#4974. Ansem Meme Coin Crashes After $2.57 Million Wallet Drain, Bullpen Confirms Security Breach

Ansem Meme Coin Crashes After $2.57 Million Wallet Drain, Bullpen Confirms Security Breach

Crypto trading platform Bullpen confirmed a security incident on Tuesday after a wallet belonging to popular crypto influencer Ansem dumped millions of dollars worth of meme coins, which led to accusations that the trader had deliberately sold his holdings and blamed hackers.

The incident sent The Black Bull, a Solana meme coin that trades as ANSEM named after the influencer, crashing roughly 60% in less than an hour. An on-chain investigation subsequently identified $2.57 million in funds transferred to a wallet on Arbitrum.

“On November 24, we identified unauthorized transfers involving Bullpen accounts opened during our early beta between April and June 2024,” the company said on X. “Our preliminary count is 18–19 affected accounts, including [Ansem’s].”

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Solana with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

The announcement lends credibility to Ansem's explanation of what happened earlier Tuesday, when blockchain trackers spotted his wallet rapidly liquidating its meme coin holdings.

“Pump wallet is hacked, trying to figure out how, believe its unauthorized access to my bullpen profile somehow which had the sol priv key imported,” Ansem wrote on X.

Bullpen, a crypto trading terminal co-founded by Ansem himself, allows traders to import existing wallets using their private keys. Anyone who obtains that key can effectively take control of the corresponding wallet, signing transactions that the blockchain recognizes as legitimate regardless of who initiated them.

A subsequent investigation by blockchain data provider Bitquery identified moved funds at $2.57 million total, with approximately $2.1 million coming from meme coin sales.

Ansem's explanation initially met considerable skepticism from crypto traders and blockchain researchers, some of whom pointed to what appeared to be connections between the recipient wallet and the influencer's older addresses.

“Pretty sure Ansem didn’t get hacked lol,” pseudonymous blockchain researcher MLM wrote on X.

“The onchain activity looks nothing like a hack,” he added. “Just an hour before the selling started, a previously inactive wallet I’d labeled as Ansem’s a year ago funded the wallet that later received the sale proceeds.”

A proposed Community Note on Ansem's post went considerably further, accusing the influencer of deliberately liquidating his position and transferring the proceeds to his own wallets. The note even drew a comparison with Haliey Welch, the internet celebrity behind the controversial HAWK meme coin.

The note was still awaiting additional ratings.

Ansem rose to prominence during the 2024 meme coin frenzy thanks in part to his calls on tokens such as Dogwifhat (WIF). Decrypt named him among its rising crypto stars that year, when his following had grown to approximately 600,000 accounts on X.

His namesake token debuted on the Solana meme coin factory Pump.fun in June 2026 after an anonymous developer created the coin and allocated a substantial portion of its supply to the influencer.

There were also reasons to question the accusations against Ansem before Bullpen issued its statement. Bitquery found that an older Solana wallet was emptied around the same time as his main wallet, potentially explaining why an address previously associated with the trader had funded the recipient.

Meanwhile, his Hyperliquid trading account, which held approximately $373,000, remained untouched. Someone with access exclusively to his Solana private keys would not necessarily have access to that account.

Bullpen said the affected accounts represent less than 0.005% of its registered user base. The company has yet to disclose the precise vulnerability, the total losses across affected accounts, or whether it intends to compensate users.

“We’ve taken the affected test service offline,” Bullpen said, adding that it would contact affected users directly and provide updates every three hours throughout the investigation.

#4973. The Best Matching Sweat Sets, Tested by Style and Fitness Editors

Just in time for Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Back in the day, a sweatsuit was all about comfort. It wasn’t so much a fashion staple, but the kind of thing to throw on and lounge in. With Y2K style back in vogue, matching sweatsuits are more commonplace than ever—just with a little less sparkle than the ones previously sported by icons like Paris Hilton and J.Lo in the early 2000s. And, with the rise of athleisure, these simple sweats have gotten the luxury treatment: they’re softer, more flattering, and pricier than ever.

Whether you’re the kind of person who considers it a cozy wardrobe essential, or you’re just looking to treat yourself to something comfortable to wear around the house, there have never been more choices when it comes to the best matching sweatsuits. Since we’re heading into winter (and Black Friday is just around the corner!), Women’s Health editors tested the most popular styles.

Here are our thoughts on the matching sets after months of lounging in them, working from home in them, and even wearing them to work.

Oner Active’s workout clothes have had our hearts at WH for a while. That’s why we were excited to put their loungewear to the test. Associate Health and Fitness editor Addison Aloian wore this set while traveling, chilling at home, and even working behind the scenes on a photoshoot.

“I absolutely love this set from Oner,” she says. She loves it for its comfort, warmth, and versatility (Aloian says she knows she could wear it outside in the chilly NYC winter, layer it under her ski clothes, or pop it on over leggings for her warm-up at the gym). “But the standout feature is the color,” Aloian says. “So many sweat sets are gray or black, but the turquoise is stunning and makes it a standout in my closet when I want a monochromatic moment.” She opted for the “oil blue” color, but Oner also has options like alpine green and toasted red, plus your neutral staples.

It’s also one of the more affordable options we tested—and on sale for half off this Black Friday. But that doesn’t mean it skimps on quality: The material feels super plush since it’s made from 67% cotton and 33% polyester, for a super plush feel that doesn’t pill or shed after one wash.

The set’s one flaw? The bottoms are a little long. At 5 '1, Aloian says she’d love a “short” option as well. Oner does offer a “long” length, though, for the taller girlies.

Old Navy Bounce Fleece Half-Zip Pullover Sweatshirt

Old Navy High-Waisted Bounce Fleece Jogger Sweatpants

In a world of expensive sweat sets, Old Navy’s Bounce Fleece line provides a budget-friendly—and stylish—option. “You’d never know these are super affordable,” says Fitness editor Cori Ritchey. They hold their own with the rest of the pricier sets from their fit to their feel.

The highlight for Ritchey is the material, a mix of polyester, rayon, and spandex. “It moves with you, and the fabric feels like it breathes compared to other sweatsuits that feel too heavy and hot.” One small caveat: Be sure to follow the wash instructions and keep your cycle on cold and gentle, tumble dry low, and keep the garments inside out. Ritchey says she noticed a bit of pilling after the first wash, but says that after following the wash instructions during the next few washes, the set stayed in great shape.

The half-zip and jogger combo makes for a put-together look and is cozy enough for traveling, running errands, or lounging around the house, Ritchey says. The set comes in plenty of neutral colors, plus some fun ones like orchid. It’s also the first on our list that doesn’t have a prominent logo, for anyone who wants a clean-looking set with no branding. Another point for Old Navy: It’s the most size-inclusive on the list. Sizing goes from XS to 4XL, with regular, tall, and petite options.

Alo is another longtime favorite at WH. The brand is known for its cozy, stylish (and premium-priced) loungewear. The fit is what we love most. The set, which comes in over a dozen colors, has an oversized feel, yet still manages to look intentional, says Deputy Features editor Carina Hsieh. “Unlike other sweatsuits, this one doesn’t look or feel unflattering or sloppy,” she says. She especially likes how it falls on her shoulders.

It’s also the “perfect transition-weather sweatsuit.” The French terry material is made up of 65% cotton and 35% polyester, for a “really soft, thick, and high-quality” feel. The fabric doesn’t feel ultra-heavy, though, so it’s a great pick for fall and spring when you might overheat in thicker sets. Another perk? The pants have pockets.

However, the sizing isn’t the most intuitive. Hsieh, who is typically a small or medium in other brands, is an extra-extra small in these pants. The pants also run a bit long. Hsieh says sizing down is likely the way to go for this set.

Aritzia Cozy Sweatfleece Mega Funnel Neck

I had been hearing great things about Aritzia’s Sweatfleece line, and after testing for over a month, I can attest that it’s truly the coziest sweat set I’ve worn. Made from 78% cotton and 22% polyester, the material is soft with a fleece-lined interior. They’ll definitely keep you warm; that fleece inside is perfect for chilly temps. But they don’t feel too heavy. The material is still breathable, and I don’t get overheated when I’m wearing them.

I also love the look of this set, especially with the funnel/mockneck style—which is very on-trend. I have been wearing the suit when I work from home, and it makes me feel put together and chic, even though I’m in the coziest clothes I own. I’m also a runner, and I've noticed that this is the first thing I want to put on after I shower post-run. It’s the ultimate comfy outfit for recovery.

When it comes to sizing, these sweats have a “mega” fit, which means they’re oversized. I still sized up just to make sure mine would be roomy, but learned that I didn’t need to. These give you an oversized fit at your true size. Plus, as a shorter girlie (5’2!), I was thrilled that they came in short, regular, and long lengths. They’re still just the tiniest bit long, so I flip the elastic on each ankle under to shorten the legs. You can’t tell a thing!

Set Active Staple SET Uniform Layered Crewneck

Set Active Staple Straight Leg Sweatpants

This vintage-inspired sweatsuit from Set Active is made from 100% cotton, for those who want to prioritize more natural fibers. “I love how soft they feel,” Hsieh says. “Sometimes 100% cotton feels stiff to me, and I’ve found that cotton sweats in particular lay weirdly at the chest when they’re oversized, but these maintain their plushy softness.”

This set is mid-weight, cozy, and warm. “I love a crewneck and sweatpants to sleep in, but sometimes find other sweats to be too much underneath my many layers of comforter and other blankets. These are the perfect weight to be warm and let me sleep comfortably,” Hsieh says. The crewneck isn't too bulky either—a challenge for a lot of sweatshirts—and fits easily underneath a jacket.

This set comes in tons of bold colorways, with contrasting collars and retro logos on the crewneck—so it’s great for anybody who's into the vintage activewear look. The only con? Hsieh, who is 5’3, found that pants run slightly long.

lululemon Scuba Oversized Full-Zip Hoodie

This lululemon hoodie was named the best zip-up in our guide to the best hoodies for its comfy, classic fit. Where the hoodie shines, according to Associate Style & Commerce Editor Shannen Zitz, the pants are just as impressive. Both stand out for the waffle material: A soft, stretchy blend of cotton, modal, and polyester. She finds it more breathable than some of her buttery-smooth cotton sweats. Another perk? It’s basically immune to pilling.

“Both pieces are incredibly soft and cozy,” Zitz says. “I love the slightly oversized, waist-length fit of the top. It pairs really well with the matching sweatpants, which are equally comfy and have a flattering drape with a straight-leg fit.”

This set styled with a plain white tee underneath and a pair of comfortable sneakers “happens to be my travel fit of choice,” she says. “The hoodie keeps me warm and cozy during cold flights and early morning departure days, but I can easily unzip it or tie it around my waist if I get too warm.”

The Restore hoodie is one of Vuori’s best sellers, and for good reason. “I love the material,” Richey says. “It’s very soft and feels super durable.” The French terry material (a cotton blend that’s smooth on the outside with brushed fleece on the inside)is made of breathable cotton and sturdy polyester.

As far as sweat sets go, this one has a lot of heft. The Restore line is thicker and denser than the label's BlissBlend or DreamKnit lines, making this set incredibly warm with a high-quality, structured feel. “The softness seems to also stay wash after wash, which is a huge win!” Richey adds.

When it comes to fit, the hoodie has a perfectly oversized shape, but you might benefit from sizing up in the bottoms, particularly if you’re thicker-thighed, Ritchey says. The pant comes in short, regular, and long lengths, giving you even more options to find the right fit.

This Spanx set stands out as a lighter-weight and more polished option. “This set feels so light and airy,” says Zitz. Spanx’s Air Essentials is made of their signature Spacer Fabric (a blend of modal, polyester, and elastane), for an ultra-smooth feel with plenty of stretch.

“It’s one of the most comfortable lounge sets I own, but also one of the nicest looking,” Zitz says. The structured half-zip top and tailored (yet roomy) wide-leg pant have an almost dressed-up look, so you can wear the set to lounge or out of the house. It also comes in nearly 20 colors—a range of neutrals to bright options like red, blue, and plum.

There is one downside: Neither the top nor bottom has pockets. While they might take away from the streamlined look, being able to slip your phone or wallet into a small pocket would be a bonus.

Gap VintageSoft Oversized Henley Pullover

Gap VintageSoft Baggy Wide-Leg Sweatpants

Gap certainly holds its own in the loungewear category. Aside from the cozy feel (thanks to a blend of cotton and polyester), it really shines when it comes to style.

“I love a wide-leg sweatpant,” Zitz says. “I find they look less loungey than a jogger, and this pair is roomy without swallowing up my entire frame.” Even better is the henley top: The button-up design and mock neck make this top look more chic than your average crewneck or half-zip. “It’s unlike any other sweatshirt I own in terms of style,” Zitz says.

One area for improvement: The color options. Our tester opted for a soft blue color, but would have preferred a more neutral gray—it just wasn’t in stock due to the limited colorways.

Rhone is another label that the WH fitness and style editors love. I have personally been a fan of their DreamGlow line for a while. It’s warm, but also has a sleek feel to it. There’s no heaviness to this set at all.

Made primarily of polyester and a small amount of elastane, the fabric also contains lyocell, a semi-synthetic fiber that helps to wick moisture away from the body, creating a slightly cooling effect. This set is ideal for anyone who runs hot or for transitional spring or fall weather. I like to wear it around my apartment on work-from-home days or as a travel outfit.

This is also the set for someone who is a little sweatsuit-reluctant. The top has a slightly cropped and boxy fit, while the pants are a barrel-leg shape (a.k.a. a flared mid-leg and tapered ankle). Combined with the ultra-smooth material, this set looks less frumpy than your old-school sweat suits.

#4970. Hong Kong Monetary Authority launches digital asset platform for tokenized debt securities

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

HSBC, Standard Chartered, Bank of China (HK), DBS, and six other banks are the first direct participants.

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority has launched the CMU Digital Asset Platform designed to facilitate the issuance, settlement, and tokenization of debt securities, as the region continues to embrace tokenized assets in its push to become a crypto hub.

In a statement released Wednesday, Hong Kong's de facto central bank said that the new platform supports the paperless process spanning debt securities issuance, clearing, and settlement. It also adopts an atomic delivery-versus-payment onchain settlement model, providing 24-hour settlement in multi-currencies using cash tokens.

The platform's capabilities were "validated" through trial trades in tokenized Exchange Fund Bills earlier this year, CMU OmniClear said in a separate statement.

Established in 2024, CMU OmniClear operates and develops Hong Kong’s Central Moneymarkets Unit system on behalf of the HKMA. The central securities depository had more than HK$6 trillion ($765.5 billion) in assets under custody as of the end of September.

CMU OmniClear plans to explore expanding the platform beyond debt securities to other asset classes, including funds and real-world assets, according to the statement. It will also explore opportunities to integrate with other decentralized platforms and instruments, including tokenized deposits and regulated stablecoins.

The first batch of direct participants are HSBC, Standard Chartered, Bank of China (HK), DBS, and six other banks, per the statement.

"CMU OmniClear is implementing a strategic roadmap to establish the CMU as the core infrastructure for a multi-asset digital financial ecosystem in Hong Kong," Eddie Yue, chief executive of the HKMA, said in the statement. "This also creates synergies with HKMA's digital payment initiatives, facilitating efficient and secure end-to-end processes for digital assets."

"Partnering with industry stakeholders, we will actively expand use cases, diversify asset class coverage, and connect with broader payment rails and other DLT platforms to create a future-proof ecosystem that defines the next generation of digital finance," said Stanley Chan, CEO of CMU OmniClear.

Hong Kong is ramping up efforts to develop its digital asset ecosystem, particularly as tokenized assets gain traction.

In June, the HKMA formed an expert group to drive the development of tokenized bonds. It is also exploring the use of agentic AI to monitor crypto asset transactions and detect money-laundering risks, Executive Director Raymond Chan said last week.

Elsewhere in Asia, Singapore's OCBC Bank launched a pilot with StraitsX on Monday for cross-border business-to-business stablecoin payments. Last week, the Monetary Authority of Singapore announced that it issued S$100 million ($77.5 million) of four-week tokenized MAS Bills on Nov. 6.

#4968. What Is Pons? The Robinhood Chain Meme Coin Launchpad Explained

What Is Pons? The Robinhood Chain Meme Coin Launchpad Explained

When Robinhood switched on its own Robinhood Chain blockchain on July 1, 2026, the trading app's stock tokens were supposed to be the main attraction. Instead, much of the early activity came from meme coins: tokens built around a joke or an internet trend.

Pons became the busiest place to make them. Like Pump.fun on Solana, it lets anyone pick a name, ticker and image and have a tradable token minutes later, without writing code. Its fees briefly made it one of the highest-earning protocols in crypto, and its own token, PONS, went on to list on Kraken and Coinbase.

That openness can also be exploited. In September 2026, an onchain analyst alleged that one group had used Pons launches to extract millions of dollars from buyers.

This guide explains what Pons is, how its two generations of contracts work, what the PONS token does, and the risks.

Pons is a token launch protocol running on Robinhood Chain, a layer-2 network built on Ethereum using Arbitrum's technology, and its website and documentation are published by Pons Labs, LLC.

Every token launched through Pons is a standard ERC-20 token with a fixed supply, 1 billion tokens on V1 launches, that can never be increased. The creator gets no allocation set aside before trading opens.

Pons is also non-custodial. Its documentation says every launch and trade is a transaction the user's own wallet signs, and the platform never holds user funds.

Pons went live within days of Robinhood Chain's mainnet. It picked up most of the chain's launchpad activity after an early rival, Noxa, stopped accepting new launches on July 11, 2026, according to Decrypt's reporting.

Pons has two generations of contracts, V1 and V2, and both remain live on Robinhood Chain.

In V1, a single transaction deploys the token and its trading pool, a Uniswap V3 pool paired with wrapped ETH (WETH), and locks the pool's liquidity so the creator can't withdraw it. Each launch costs 0.0005 ETH and carries a 1% trading fee, the documentation says. A launch "graduates" once 4.2 ETH has been paired in its pool by default, but trading carries on in the same pool.

V1 launches are protected for their first two blocks: in the launch block, only the creator's initial buy can execute, and for the rest of the window no wallet can hold more than 5% of supply or buy more than 5.5%. Fees are split 70% to the creator and 30% to the protocol for current launches.

V2 adds a bonding curve: a contract that holds a token's whole supply and sets its price by formula, rising as people buy and falling as they sell. According to the V2 documentation, the curve sells out, then "graduates" automatically into a Uniswap V4 pool, seeded with a fixed share of supply held back from the start. The pool's liquidity is then locked permanently; no unlock function exists.

V2 launches can be priced in ETH or in other assets Pons has approved, including tokenized stocks, in which case the creator is paid in that asset. Each trade pays a standard fee shared between Pons, the creator and an optional buyback, plus an optional creator tax that is capped by the protocol and fixed at launch.

When a creator turns buybacks on, part of their own fee is spent buying their token back. Those tokens are locked in a vault and released over five years, split between the creator and the protocol.

PONS itself was launched through Pons's own legacy V1 factory, and its documentation uses PONS as the reference token for developers testing their integrations.

"Sniping" means buying a large share of a new token in its first seconds, often with bots, then selling into later buyers. Every V2 launch opens with a "snipe tax" of 99% on buys that decays to zero over five seconds, the documentation says.

The launching wallet and the creator's fee wallet are exempt automatically, and creators can name up to 32 more exempt addresses at launch "for a team bundling its opening buys across several wallets."

That exemption became central to allegations published on September 27, 2026. Pseudonymous onchain analyst Wazz tweeted that a single operation had extracted at least $18.43 million from 53 Robinhood Chain launches between July 10 and September 21, 2026, mostly through Pons V2. Wazz said nearly every launch was sniped for 70% or more of its supply by bundles of 70 to 200 wallets.

I just uncovered the biggest serial Rugpulling and Extraction operation on Robinhood

The same operation is linked 53 launches within a 2 month period

very likely more this is just what I could directly link

🧵 https://t.co/wS62KAbvv5 pic.twitter.com/BSxZL9wU44

The Block reviewed the onchain data and found that creators of nine Pons V2 launches had exempted 15 to 25 wallets each from the snipe tax, which then bought out the bonding curve in a single transaction. The creator and those wallets held 82% to 86% of supply after the opening buys. The Block did not independently replicate Wazz's $18.43 million total.

On September 3, 2026, Pons generated $5.95 million in daily fees, briefly out-earning Robinhood Chain itself and ranking fourth among all protocols tracked by DefiLlama, Decrypt reported. Pons fees drove Robinhood Chain to a record of about $6 million in daily fees in early September 2026, The Block reported.

On September 5, 2026, blockchain analytics firm Arkham tweeted that crypto market maker Wintermute appeared to be buying PONS slowly in a series of small purchases, and held just over $3 million of the token. Wallets that Arkham attributes to Wintermute held about 3.4 million PONS at the time, and about 7.4 million as of November 2026.

As of November 20, 2026, DefiLlama put Pons's cumulative fees at about $205 million. Of that, $137 million came in September 2026 alone; fees fell to about $17 million in October 2026.

PONS is the ERC-20 token tied to the Pons launchpad, with a fixed supply of 1 billion. Its link to the platform is a buyback.

According to the V1 documentation, 80% of the protocol's fees are used to buy PONS on the market through an automated process and send it to a burn address, permanently removing it from circulation. The remaining 20% pays for infrastructure and the Pons team. Kraken's listing notice describes the same mechanism.

As of November 20, 2026, CoinGecko data shows about 669 million PONS in circulation, out of a fixed supply of 1 billion.

You can track PONS's latest price on Decrypt's price page.

PONS trades in Uniswap pools on Robinhood Chain. Binance Wallet added it to its Binance Alpha tier on September 2, 2026, and Kraken opened PONS trading on September 25, 2026, with access through the Kraken App and Instant Buy to follow once liquidity allows. Coinbase Markets tweeted on October 6, 2026, that it had added PONS to its listing roadmap, and said the next day that its PONS-USD pair would open later that day, if liquidity conditions were met.

Pons has flagged several changes still to come. Its V1 documentation says the 80% share of protocol fees used to buy back PONS is not yet fixed in its contracts, but will become "immutable, decentralized, and automated" in a future release.

On V2, three security firms (SB Security, Dingbats and Pashov Audit Group) are reviewing the contracts, and Pons says it will publish their reports in full, including any findings it did not accept, once the reviews close. Until then, its documentation tells users to treat V2 as unaudited, and only whitelisted addresses can create V2 tokens.

Pons also faces competition on its home chain. Uniswap, already Robinhood Chain's main exchange, launched its own launchpad, Pools.trade, on August 5, 2026. It charges no launchpad fee, locks each launch's liquidity permanently, and offers a "crowd launch" option designed to resist bundling. Within its first days, Pools.trade took about half of Robinhood Chain's launchpad volume, Decrypt's Morning Minute newsletter reported. The newsletter noted that Uniswap can afford to forgo launchpad fees because it earns from its other products, which most dedicated launchpads cannot.

Pons has since kept the larger share of fees. As of November 2026, DefiLlama showed Pons collecting about $5.6 million in fees over the previous 30 days, against about $115,000 for Pools.trade. The two charge different rates, though: Pools.trade's trading fee is 0.25%, while Pons's standard fee is 1%.

V2's tokenized-stock pairs link Pons launches to the stock tokens Robinhood built the chain to carry, which ties Pons's prospects to Robinhood Chain itself. On Robinhood's third-quarter earnings call on October 27, 2026, CEO Vlad Tenev said the growth of the chain and its ecosystem had exceeded the company's expectations, and that Robinhood was investing in how to support the chain's developer community.

#4967. Racerback Sports Bras Support Without Getting in the Way. These 6 Editor-Tested Picks Are the Best.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

A racerback style bra, the style in which the straps meet at the back to create an X or Y shape, happens to be a sort of Goldilocks bra option that suits most sizes because they’re super customizable. As a style writer who’s tested more bras than I can count (at different weights and sizes over the years), I’ve found that racerback sports bras tend to work especially well for smaller and larger busts alike. That’s part of why racerback bras have such a loyal following: they’re supportive, comfortable, less likely to slip around, and easy to style under a variety of workout tops.

This is especially true for bras with added features like underwire, molded cups, or a wider band, says Dani Read, a senior designer for luxury lingerie brand Cosabella. Adjustable straps (as opposed to fixed backs) can also help you get the right fit in a racerback, she adds. Racerback bras are a go-to style for Women’s Health’s style and fitness team, and for this guide, we’ve selected some of our favorites that we reach for again and again.

“My boobs lean on the larger side, so I usually go for sports bras with a higher neckline to keep everything secure (no one wants spillage mid-workout!),” says style contributor Lily Wohlner. “So when I first got this bra, I was a little skeptical.” She wasn’t sure it would 1) hold her chest up during workouts and 2) provide enough coverage. But Wohlner was pleasantly surprised and found that it actually offers a solid amount of compression, thanks to the nylon and elastane blend, which lifts and supports without feeling flimsy.

It’s become one of her favorite racerback sports bras and she’s consistently impressed by how well it holds her in during strength training classes. The cute, strappy back design definitely doesn’t hurt, either.

Another bonus: the fabric dries super quickly, so even when you break a sweat, you don’t have to worry about visible marks. It feels light and breathable, but the support is legit—like what you’d expect from a more heavy-duty bra. One thing to note: it runs a little big in the chest area. Wohlner says she probably should’ve sized down for a more snug fit. That said, her usual medium still works, it just doesn’t have that extra-tight, compressive feel some of her high-impact bras do. We also wish it had adjustable straps for customizability.

Crz Yoga makes some of the best workout clothes on Amazon we’ve tested—and the Butterluxe Racerback Sports Bra might just be the softest thing you’ll ever put on your body. Crafted from a luxurious blend of 81 percent polyamide and 19 percent lycra elastane, the signature Butterluxe fabric lives up to its name—smooth and silky. It’s perfect for low-impact workouts like yoga, barre, or stretching, and doubles as a comfy everyday bra you'll actually want to keep on.

The scoop neckline and racerback cut give it a clean silhouette, which I love to wear on its own or layered, while the removable pads offer customizable coverage. It’s also moisture-wicking and breathable, so you stay cool and dry when the heat kicks in. If you’re after a bra that feels like a second skin but still holds it together, this one’s a top player.

This top leans more tank than bra, but with a built-in shelf bra, it's the two-in-one you didn’t know you needed—which is why it earned the top spot in our guide to the best workout tops and is a personal fave of mine. It’s made from a soft blend of polyester and elastane, making it the comfiest option in this guide (and definitely the lightest!). Honestly, it feels like you're wearing nothing at all, but it still keeps the girls in place with just a touch of compression for light movement. The cherry on top? It’s moisture-wicking, so it keeps you dry whether you’re working out or just running around on a hot day.

That said, it’s not the most supportive option here. I usually throw it on for errands or walks, where I don’t need much hold. I wouldn’t wear it by itself to a workout class with a lot of jumping because there’s potential for some serious spillage. If you have a bigger chest, you’ll probably want to layer a sports bra underneath. But if you're part of the itty bitty titty committee, you're good to go wearing this solo pretty much anywhere.

This bra is my go-to and a favorite of health and fitness director Jacqueline Andriakos because it’s incredibly supportive without feeling overly tight. It’s made with Revive, a super soft, midweight stretch fabric (a blend of nylon and spandex) that hugs your body just right. The chafe-free seams and built-in shelf bra add even more comfort and support during workouts.

Andriakos likes wearing it for low-impact workouts like Pilates or yoga, since it’s not overly compressive, but for me, the medium support still holds up for activities like jogging or strength training—especially for a small-to-medium bust. However, if you have a larger bust, I still recommend this bra because it has nice coverage, but I don’t know how supportive it would be for higher-impact activity.

When things get sweaty, the moisture-wicking fabric and built-in anti-odor technology keep you feeling fresh. Just a heads-up: it runs small, so consider sizing up if you prefer a less snug fit. That said, I actually don’t mind the tighter feel when I’m in the mood for extra support.

If you’re after a racerback bra that will support you through any move, the On Performance Flex Bra deserves a spot in your drawer. Designed with soft, breathable materials that have compression, this bra is perfect for high-impact workouts like running, boxing, and HIIT.

The Performance Flex Bra is made with a buttery-soft blend of recycled polyamide and elastane, offering a nice hug that moves with you. It has that sleek racerback cut with no underwires or fastening that allows for full range of motion without digging in. Plus, it features a supportive underband and molded cups (removable!) that give you shape without feeling bulky. I love that said underband stays put without riding up or creating weird lines under clothes. It’s sweat-wicking and quick-drying, so you’ll stay dry and comfortable through everything from HIIT to running.

It runs a little snug, so if you’re between sizes or prefer a more relaxed fit, you might want to size up.

This bra is made with a polyamide and elastane blend, which is soft, breathable, and stretchy. I swear by this option and wear it daily for low-key outings and low-impact workouts. The elasticized band and adjustable straps are way easier to put on than underwire bras, and offer just enough support for daily wear, though it doesn’t have quite enough compression for high-impact workouts. It also doesn’t dig in, unlike other bralettes I’ve tried—after wearing Skims’ racerback, I rarely ever reach for a wired bra.

Just one thing: This bra runs a bit small. According to the size guide online, I should be a medium, but I needed to snag the large for a comfortable fit. That said, the bra is available in sizes up to a 4XL (or around an H-cup).

Our experts say that the most important consideration in selecting any type of bra—racerback or otherwise—is finding the right size. And, unfortunately, sometimes you may not be able to find your size at any old retailer. Most stores only stock "standard sizes"—that is, sizes 32-38 B-D, says Laura Burke, intimate apparel stylist and certified bra fit expert. But inclusive bra sizes go as large as an N cup, she says, so keep an eye out for a wider range of sizes when you're shopping if you need to. And remember: You may have to visit a bra boutique to find sizes on the far end of the spectrum.

When it comes to racerback styles, Read recommends adjustable straps, particularly if you're larger-chested and know you need more support. "The strap placement should have the straps sitting comfortably on your shoulders," she says. The correct strap placement helps alleviate pressure on the shoulders and distribute the weight of your bust evenly, preventing back pain.
